## Appendix A The formal mathematics underlying ridges

We now discuss the formal mathematical definition and several important geometrical properties of the ridges. We also emphasize its connection with caustics and envelopes that play a fundamental role in geometrical optics.

### A.1 Brief summary of the relevant ideas from differential geometry of surfaces

We need a few essential definitions from the theory of surfaces in differential geometry (Struik, 2012; Koenderink, 1990; Bruce and Giblin, 1992) before we can proceed.

On a smooth surface (say of constant flux $\psi$ ), parametrized by local coordinates $\bm{r}=(u,v)$ at each point $\bm{P}$ , we can define a unit normal $\bm{N}$ , which coincides with $\bm{\nabla}\psi/|\bm{\nabla}\psi|$ at a non-critical point where $|\bm{\nabla}\psi|\neq 0$ . The map from a point to its normal is the Gauss map. The first and second fundamental forms of the surface are defined as

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{I}\equiv d\bm{r}\cdot d\bm{r}=g_{ij}dr^{i}dr^{j},\quad\mathrm{II}\equiv-d\bm{r}\cdot d\bm{N}. $$

The shape operator can be obtained through the $(u,v)$ derivatives of $\bm{N}$ as $S(\bm{r}_{,u})=-\bm{N}_{,u}$ and $S(\bm{r}_{,v})=-\bm{N}_{,v}$ . The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the shape operator gives the principal curvatures $(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2})$ and principal directions $(\bm{e}_{1},\bm{e}_{2})$ . The Gaussian curvature $K_{G}\equiv\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}$ , and the mean curvature $H=(\kappa_{1}+\kappa_{2})/2$ are the determinant and half the trace of the shape operator.

The parabolic line with $K_{G}=0$ when either $\kappa_{1}=0$ or $\kappa_{2}=0$ , is the surface analogs of inflection points. It separates the hyperbolic $K_{G}<0$ region and the elliptic $K_{G}>0$ region. The Gauss map has singularities on the parabolic line as the determinant of the shape operator vanish along the line.

The asymptotic direction consists of directions along which $\mathrm{II}$ vanish identically. Asymptotic curves are curves with tangent in the asymptotic direction, for which the normal curvature is always zero. Asymptotic curves exist only in $K_{G}\leq 0$ regions. For $K_{G}<0$ , a pair of asymptotic curves exist, while on the parabolic line $K_{G}=0$ , there is only one. An asymptotic inflection point is a point where the asymptotic curve has zero geodesic curvature. Since by definition, asymptotic curves have zero normal curvatures, at the inflection points, they are straight lines. Thus, any straight line on a surface must be an asymptotic curve with degenerate inflection points.

At points called umbilical points, the two principal curvatures are equal. The ratio of the two principal curvatures typically scales as the aspect ratio of the device. Since in a stellarator, the aspect ratio is always larger than one, even for the most compact designs, the principal curvatures are almost always unequal. Thus, umbilical points are rare and will be ignored henceforth.

### A.2 Formal definition of ridges and ridge points

Formally, ridges are defined as a collection of ridge points at which one of the principal curvatures attains an extremum along the corresponding principal direction (Porteous, 2001; Koenderink, 1990). Thus, curves along which $\bm{e}_{1}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\kappa_{1}=0$ or $\bm{e}_{2}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\kappa_{2}=0$ defines ridges. Being an extrema of a principal curvature, ridge points are analogs of vertices of planar curves (Bruce and Giblin, 1992), where the curvature has a local extremum.

Closely associated with planar vertices is the concept of an evolute (Arnold, 1990), which is defined as the envelope to the normals to the curve. In the case of a planar curve, the evolute is obtained by joining all points that are located at normal distances from the curve equal to the radii of curvature. Evolutes have cusp singularities near the vertices. In other words, on a planar curve, the vertices are also points that are closest to the cusp singularity of the evolute to the curve.

The surface analog of an evolute is obtained from the loci of the two principal curvatures. Hence, there are typically two of these surfaces, which are also called caustic surfaces or focal surfaces (Porteous, 2001; Koenderink, 1990).

The caustic surfaces can have singularities such as cusp points or cuspidal edges called ribs (Porteous, 2001). At these singularities, two or more normals meet. Ridge points are the surface analogs of planar curve vertices in the sense that they are the closest points on the surface to the cusp singularities of the caustic surface, the distance between them scaling inversely with the curvature.

### A.3 Connection with caustics

Caustics play an important role in optics (Berry, 1976; Berry and others, 1981), and are defined as surfaces where two or more rays meet such that the formal geometrical optics breakdown leads to formally infinite intensity of light. The meeting of rays in a caustic signals a characteristic degeneracy that play a crucial role in the theory of rainbows and ship wakes (Berry and Howls, 2010).

We illustrate the underlying mechanism for the formation of caustics in optics with the example of asymptotic approximations of oscillatory integrals typical in WKB theory. The method of stationary phase allows one to expand the oscillatory integral near a critical point up to quadratic terms and evaluate the resulting Gaussian integral analytically. As a result, we obtain the square root of the second derivative of the phase in the denominator. However, if the critical point is degenerate, the second derivative of the phase goes to zero. This happens precisely near the turning points in WKB theory where incident, reflected and transmitted “rays” can coexist. Near such degenerate critical points, the amplitude of the Gaussian approximation formally blows up, which is the essence of a caustic formation. Near turning points, we need the third order terms in the phase to obtain a finite approximation of the integral in terms of Airy functions.

The mathematical machinery needed for treating caustics self-consistently is catastrophe theory (Arnold et al., 1986; Berry, 1976; Berry and Upstill, 1980; Poston and Stewart, 2014). Due to the association with caustics, the description of ridges requires similar tools (Porteous, 2001; Koenderink, 1990), which we discuss in further details in our forthcoming paper. In the following, we briefly summarize relevant known results from Banchoff et al. (1982).

The singularities of the Gauss map that happens on the parabolic curves have deep connection with ridges. Banchoff, Gaffney, and McCrory Banchoff et al. (1982) shows that the generic singularities of the Gauss map are folds and cusps. Typically, lines of curvature $\bm{e}_{i}$ cross asymptotic lines transversely at folds. However, at the cusp they are tangential. Gaussian cusps occur precisely where the ridge lines cross the parabolic curve with vanishing principal curvature. The inflection points on the asymptotic lines also accumulate near the cusps of Gauss, essentially requiring the asymptotic lines to be straight. Asymptotic lines approach the parabolic curve and are tangent to it at the cusp. The parabolic curves thus serves as a local envelope to all the asymptotic curves near the cusp of Gauss.

### A.4 Implications for stellarators

We now emphasize certain key differences between regular X point of a tokamak or a resonant island and the 3D ridges in stellarators that arises due to caustics.

Magnetic field lines are essentially straight and therefore asymptotic lines in the vicinity of the ridges, as we have shown using the optical analogy. They approach the parabolic line but can not cross since $K_{G}$ mus be negative and so stay tangential. Thus, the parabolic curves form an envelope along the ridge. As we saw in the last Section, this configuration is the signature of the cusp of Gauss. The essential point to note here is that the vanishing of the field line normal on the inboard side with $B=B_{M},K_{G}<0$ is highly nontrivial and does not happen in regular X points.

Next, we note that in both these cases, $|\bm{\nabla}\psi|\to 0$ , implying that the X-point or the ridge point is a fixed point. For regular X-points, the fixed point is not degenerate since the Jacobian of the second order derivatives of $\psi$ does not vanish. For instance, from the normal form of $\psi$ near a regular X point, $\psi=B_{0}(\ell)(y^{2}-x^{2})/2$ , yields a non-vanishing Jacobian $|\partial(\psi_{,x},\psi_{,y})/\partial(x,y)|=B_{0}^{2}\neq 0$ . However, the form $\psi=B_{0}(y^{2}-x^{3})$ that can occur near cusps (Brown et al., 2025) is degenerate.

## Appendix B Differential geometric characteristics of the sharp ridges

We explore the differential geometric constraints of having a sharp ridge on a flux surface in this Appendix. We start with a parametric representation of the flux surface such that the parametric curves are orthogonal (p. 130 Struik (2012)). The first fundamental form is

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{I}=E\,du^{2}+G\,dv^{2},\qquad(F=0), $$

with arc-length parameters

$$ \displaystyle s_{1}=\int\!\sqrt{E}\,du,\qquad s_{2}=\int\!\sqrt{G}\,dv. $$

The geodesic curvatures of the coordinate curves are

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{g_{1}} \displaystyle=\bigl(\kappa_{g}\bigr)_{v=\mathrm{const}}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{E_{v}}{E\sqrt{G}}=-\frac{d}{ds_{2}}\ln\sqrt{E}, \displaystyle\kappa_{g_{2}} \displaystyle=\bigl(\kappa_{g}\bigr)_{u=\mathrm{const}}=+\frac{1}{2}\frac{G_{u}}{G\sqrt{E}}=+\frac{d}{ds_{1}}\ln\sqrt{G}. $$

Taking lines of curvature as coordinates ( $F=f=0$ ), both fundamental forms can be diagonalized (p. 113 Struik (2012))

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{I}=E\,du^{2}+G\,dv^{2},\qquad\mathrm{II}=e\,du^{2}+g\,dv^{2}. $$

The principal curvatures are

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{1}=\frac{e}{E},\qquad\kappa_{2}=\frac{g}{G}. $$

In these coordinates, the Codazzi–Mainardi Equations are

$$ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{G}}\dfrac{\partial\kappa_{1}}{\partial v}=+\dfrac{(\kappa_{2}-\kappa_{1})}{2}\dfrac{E_{v}}{E\sqrt{G}},\qquad\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{E}}\dfrac{\partial\kappa_{2}}{\partial u}=-\dfrac{(\kappa_{2}-\kappa_{1})}{2}\dfrac{G_{u}}{G\sqrt{E}}. $$

Rewriting in arc-length coordinates ( $\partial_{s_{1}}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{E}}\,\partial_{u},\partial_{s_{2}}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{G}}\,\partial_{v}$ ), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\kappa_{1}}{\partial s_{2}}=-(\kappa_{2}-\kappa_{1})\,\kappa_{g_{1}},\quad\frac{\partial\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}}=-(\kappa_{2}-\kappa_{1})\,\kappa_{g_{2}}. $$

The Gaussian Curvature ( $K_{G}$ ) for orthogonal coordinates is

$$ \displaystyle K_{G}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{EG}}\!\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\!\left(\frac{\partial\sqrt{G}}{\partial s_{1}}\right)+\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\!\left(\frac{\partial\sqrt{E}}{\partial s_{2}}\right)\right]. $$

Using $\partial_{u}=\sqrt{E}\,\partial_{s_{1}}$ , $\partial_{v}=\sqrt{G}\,\partial_{s_{2}}$ and (B.3), the expression for $K=\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}$ reduces to

$$ \displaystyle K_{G} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{G}}\,\partial_{s_{1}}\!\left(\sqrt{G}\,\kappa_{g_{2}}\right)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{E}}\,\partial_{s_{2}}\!\left(\sqrt{E}\,\kappa_{g_{1}}\right) \displaystyle=\partial_{s_{2}}\kappa_{g_{1}}-\kappa_{g_{1}}^{2}-\bigl(\partial_{s_{1}}\kappa_{g_{2}}+\kappa_{g_{2}}^{2}\bigr) $$

Until now, everything follows from basic differential geometry in local principal curvature coordinates. Now, we focus on the ridge conditions. Ridges of the principal curvatures are defined by

$$ \displaystyle\dfrac{\partial\kappa_{i}}{\partial s_{i}}=0,\quad\dfrac{\partial^{2}\kappa_{i}}{\partial s_{i}^{2}}\neq 0,\quad i=1,2. $$

We now utilize the sharpness of the ridge by assuming $\kappa_{2}\gg\kappa_{1}$ . We proved (using continuity) that field lines must align with the ridges. This implies that as $\kappa_{2}\to\infty$ , the field lines must align with the $u$ -lines, which are lines of principal curvature $\kappa_{1}$ . Thus, $s_{1}$ is along $\bm{\hat{t}}=\bm{B}/B$ and $s_{2}$ is along $\bm{\hat{b}}=\bm{\hat{t}}\times\bm{\hat{n}},\bm{\hat{n}}=\nabla\psi/|\nabla\psi|$ . The alignment of the field lines with the sharp ridges continue as long as the ridge stays sharp.

Since $\kappa_{2}\gg\kappa_{1}$ , equations (B.6) simplify to

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\kappa_{1}}{\partial s_{2}}=-\kappa_{2}\,\kappa_{g_{1}},\quad\frac{\partial\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}}=-\kappa_{2}\,\kappa_{g_{2}}. $$

Since $\kappa_{2}\gg\kappa_{1}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\kappa_{g_{1}}|\to 0, $$

as long as $\partial_{s_{2}}\kappa_{1}$ is bounded. The boundedness assumption of $\partial_{s_{2}}\kappa_{1}$ will be later demonstrated to be self-consistent. The vanishing geodesic curvature of $\bm{B}$ means the field lines are geodesics on the flux. Therefore, surface:

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{g_{1}}\to 0\;\Longrightarrow\;\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=0\;\Longrightarrow\;B\;\text{is constant along }s_{1}. $$

Combined with quasi-axisymmetry (QA), $\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=0$ implies $B$ is constant along two directions.

Next, we analyze the relation between $\kappa_{g_{2}}$ and $\kappa_{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle-\kappa_{g_{2}}=\frac{1}{\kappa_{2}}\frac{\partial\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}}=\partial_{s_{1}}\ln\kappa_{2}. $$

In general for $\kappa_{g_{2}}\neq 0$ , we can integrate (B.14) to get

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{2}=\kappa_{20}\exp\!\left(-\!\int\!\kappa_{g_{2}}\,ds_{1}\right). $$

We mow make a local approximation near a localized maximum of a $\kappa_{2}$ -ridge, such that both first derivatives vanish of $\kappa_{2}$

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}}=0,\qquad\frac{\partial\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{2}}=0. $$

From (B.6) we find that the local condition $\partial_{s_{1}}\kappa_{2}=0$ implies that $\kappa_{g_{2}}=0$ . With both $\kappa_{g_{1}}=\kappa_{g_{2}}=0$ , (B.9) reduces to $K_{G}=-\partial_{s_{1}}\kappa_{g_{2}}$ . Differentiating (B.14) with $s_{1}$ we find

$$ \displaystyle-\partial_{s_{1}}\kappa_{g_{2}}=\frac{1}{\kappa_{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}^{2}}-\left(\frac{1}{\kappa_{2}}\frac{\partial\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}}\right)^{\!2}. $$

Substitution of (B.17) into (B.9) and the restriction to the vicinity of the local maximum ( $\partial_{s_{1}}\kappa_{2}=0$ , $\;\partial_{s_{1}}^{2}\kappa_{2}<0$ ) yields a considerably simplified expression for $K_{G}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle K_{G}=\frac{1}{\kappa_{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}^{2}}\leq 0. $$

A parabolic profile of $\kappa_{2}$ in $s_{1}$ near the local maximum of $\kappa_{2}$ further implies that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}^{2}}\sim-c_{2}^{2}\,\kappa_{2}, $$

with a bounded $c_{2}$ , which physically correspond to the local value of $K_{G}$ . Since $K_{G}=\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{1}=\frac{1}{\kappa_{2}^{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}\kappa_{2}}{\partial s_{1}^{2}}=-\frac{c_{2}^{2}}{\kappa_{2}}. $$

Further, in the light of the ridge condition $\partial_{s_{2}}\kappa_{2}$ , the boundedness assumption of $\partial_{s_{2}}\kappa_{1}$ is satisfied by the $\kappa_{1}$ solution in (B.20).

Therefore, as $\kappa_{2}\to\infty$ , $\kappa_{1}\to 0$ . Since $\kappa_{1}$ is the normal curvature of $\bm{B}$ , $\kappa_{n}\to 0$ near the ridge. Since both the normal $\kappa_{n}$ and the geodesic curvature, $\kappa_{g_{1}}$ , of the magnetic field vanishes near the ridge, $\bm{B}$ must be locally straight.

## Appendix C Magnetic field lines approach asymptotic lines on the outermost surface as $B$ approaches a constant

We provide the necessary mathematical details for the Section 5.1 in this Appendix. We use the Darboux frame $(\bm{\hat{t}}=\bm{B}/B,\bm{\hat{n}}=\bm{\nabla}\psi/|\bm{\nabla}\psi|,\bm{\hat{b}}=\bm{\hat{t}}\times\bm{\hat{n}})$ consistently and start with the derivative of the $\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\psi=0$ condition,

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\hat{n}}\frac{|\bm{\nabla}\psi|}{B}+\bm{\nabla}\bm{\nabla}\psi\cdot\bm{\hat{t}}=0. $$

Dotting (C.1) with $\bm{\hat{t}}$ and using the expression for the field line curvature,

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\kappa}=\frac{\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}}{B}-\frac{\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B}{B}\bm{\hat{t}}, $$

we find that

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\kappa}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\psi+\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\bm{\nabla}\psi\cdot\bm{\hat{t}}=0, $$

which can be recast in terms of normal curvature as in (5.4).

We now prove that field lines are asymptotic curves on a constant flux surface with $\bm{\hat{t}}$ in the asymptotic direction when $\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B\to 0$ . A curve on a surface is an asymptotic curve if the second fundamental form, II, vanishes along the curve. On a flux surface $\psi$ the second fundamental form

$$ \displaystyle\text{II}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{L}\quad\mathcal{M}\\
\mathcal{M}\quad\mathcal{N}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}=-\bm{\hat{b}}\cdot\frac{\bm{\nabla}\bm{\nabla}\psi}{|\bm{\nabla}\psi|}\cdot\bm{\hat{b}},\quad\mathcal{M}=-\bm{\hat{b}}\cdot\frac{\bm{\nabla}\bm{\nabla}\psi}{|\bm{\nabla}\psi|}\cdot\bm{\hat{t}},\quad\mathcal{N}=-\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\frac{\bm{\nabla}\bm{\nabla}\psi}{|\bm{\nabla}\psi|}\cdot\bm{\hat{t}}. $$

Thus, (C.3) implies that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{N}=\kappa_{n}. $$

It is clear that when $\kappa_{n}\to 0$ , II vanishes along $\bm{\hat{t}}$ . Thus, field lines are asymptotic curves. We can express $\bm{\nabla}\bm{\nabla}\psi$ and $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ in terms of $3\times 3$ matrices in the $(\bm{\hat{n}},\bm{\hat{b}},\bm{\hat{t}})$ frame such that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{|\nabla\psi|}\bm{\nabla}\bm{\nabla}\psi=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}\quad a_{12}\quad a_{13}\\
a_{12}\quad a_{22}\quad a_{23}\\
a_{13}\quad a_{23}\quad a_{33}\end{pmatrix}\qquad\frac{\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}}{B}=\begin{pmatrix}c_{11}\quad c_{12}\quad c_{13}\\
c_{12}\quad c_{22}\quad c_{23}\\
c_{13}\quad c_{23}\quad c_{33}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Here, we have used the fact that both tensors are symmetric. The second fundamental form (C.5) from (C.7) is

$$ \displaystyle\text{II}=-\begin{pmatrix}a_{22}\quad a_{23}\\
a_{23}\quad a_{33}\end{pmatrix},\quad\text{Det(II)}=a_{22}a_{33}-a_{23}^{2}. $$

To connect the components of these tensors to physically meaningful quantities, we start from the expressions for $\kappa_{n},\kappa_{g},\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B$ given in (4.7). It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{n}=\frac{\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\hat{n}}}{B}=c_{13},\quad\kappa_{g}=\frac{\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\hat{b}}}{B}=c_{23},\quad\frac{\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B}{B}=\frac{\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\hat{t}}}{B}=c_{33}. $$

Next, $\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{B}$ implies that $c_{11}+c_{22}+c_{33}=0$ . Finally, employing (C.3), we find that

$$ \displaystyle(c_{11}\quad c_{12}\quad c_{13})+(a_{13}\quad a_{23}\quad a_{33})=0. $$

As $\kappa_{n}\to 0$ and the field line tends to an asymptotic curve, $a_{33}\to 0$ . Now,

$$ \displaystyle K_{G}=\frac{\text{Det}(II)}{\text{Det}(I)}, $$

where I,II are the first and second fundamental forms on the $\psi$ surface. From (C.8), we get $K_{G}\propto(a_{22}a_{33}-a_{23}^{2})$ . Now, as $\kappa_{n}\to 0,a_{33}\to 0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\text{II}\to-\begin{pmatrix}a_{22}\quad a_{23}\\
a_{23}\quad\;\;0\end{pmatrix},\quad\text{Det(II)}\to-\left(a_{23}\right)^{2}. $$

We now focus on the case $\kappa_{n}\to 0$ , which is appropriate near ridges as discussed in Section 4.1 and Appendix B. The vanishing $\kappa_{n}$ near $B\approx B_{M}$ is also deduced from $B_{M}^{\prime}\to 0$ in Fig 15. In the $\kappa_{n}\to 0$ limit, we examine the scenario situation where $K_{G}$ also vanish. It is clear that $a_{33},a_{23}$ both must go to zero in this limit, resulting in a highly degenerate fundamental form

$$ \displaystyle\text{II}\to-\begin{pmatrix}a_{22}\quad 0\\
0\quad\;\;0\end{pmatrix},\quad\text{Det(II)}\to 0. $$

The diagonal nature of II shows that the limiting $(\bm{\hat{b}},\bm{\hat{t}})$ are also principal curvature directions on the flux surface. Moreover, in this limit $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ takes the following form in the $(\bm{\hat{n}},\bm{\hat{b}},\bm{\hat{t}})$ basis

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}}{B}=\begin{pmatrix}c_{11}\quad\;0\qquad 0\\
\;\;0\qquad c_{22}\quad\;c_{23}\\
\;\;0\qquad c_{23}\quad\;c_{33}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Thus, the Det $(\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})/B=c_{11}(c_{22}c_{33}-c_{23}^{2})$ is clearly nonzero in general. However, because in QS, $\kappa_{g}=(G_{0}/|\bm{\nabla}\psi|)(\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B/B^{2})$ as shown in (4.8), $c_{23}=c_{33}G_{0}/|\bm{\nabla}\psi|$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\text{Det}\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}}{B}=-c_{11}c_{33}\left(c_{11}+c_{33}\left(1+\left(\frac{G_{0}}{|\bm{\nabla}\psi|}\right)^{2}\right)\right), $$

which vanishes when $\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B\to 0$ . This happens on the ridge where $\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B$ and $\bm{\hat{n}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B$ both vanish forcing $B$ to be almost a constant. Thus, we have come full circle to where we started: near almost constant $B$ , which implies

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{n}=0,\quad\bm{\hat{t}}\cdot\bm{\nabla}\kappa_{n}=0. $$

Since $\bm{\hat{t}}$ is the principal direction and $\kappa_{n}$ the curvature associated with it, (C.16) defines a ridge point, in the true mathematical sense. Moreover, it is a cusp of Gauss since $\kappa_{n}=0$ .

## Appendix D $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ tensor in axisymmetry, near closed field lines, and near ridges

### D.1 Eigenvalues of the Grad-B tensor

The $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ tensor is a $3\times 3$ matrix with real coefficients. It is traceless owing to divergence-free nature of $\bm{B}$ . Since current $\mu_{0}\bm{J}=\bm{\nabla}\times\bm{B}$ is related to the antisymmetric components of the $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$

Using Cayley-Hamilton theorem (Strang, 2006), the characteristic equation of $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{Det}(\lambda\mathbb{I}-\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})=\lambda^{3}-\mbox{Tr}(\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})\lambda^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\left(\mbox{Tr}(\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})\right)^{2}-\mbox{Tr}((\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})^{2})\right)\lambda-\mbox{Det}(\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})=0. $$

Since $\mbox{Tr}(\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})=\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{B}=0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{Det}(\lambda\mathbb{I}-\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})=\lambda^{3}+\mathcal{P}\lambda+\mathcal{Q}=0,\quad\mathcal{P}=-\frac{1}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left((\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})^{2}\right),\quad\mathcal{Q}=-\mbox{Det}(\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}). $$

The eigenvalues $\lambda_{i},i=1,2,3$ of the $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ tensor satisfy $\prod_{i}(\lambda-\lambda_{i})=0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}=0,\quad\mathcal{P}=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{2}\lambda_{3}+\lambda_{3}\lambda_{1},\quad\mathcal{Q}=-\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}\lambda_{3}. $$

It follows from the traceless condition that $2\sum_{i\neq j}\lambda_{i}\lambda_{j}+\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{2}=0$ for $i,j=1,2,3$ . Thus, $\mathcal{P}$ can also be written as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}=-\frac{1}{2}(\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{3}^{2}+\lambda_{3}^{2}). $$

Now, from the definition of the Frobenius norm, $|\mathsfbi{M}|_{F}^{2}=\mbox{Tr}(\mathsfbi{M}\mathsfbi{M}^{\top})$ and $L_{\nabla B}$ of an arbitrary symmetric tensor $\mathsfbi{M}$ we find that

$$ \displaystyle|\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}|_{F}^{2}=(\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{3}^{2}+\lambda_{3}^{2})=-2\mathcal{P}\quad\Rightarrow\quad L_{\nabla B}=\frac{\sqrt{2}B}{\sqrt{|\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}|_{F}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{P}|/B^{2}}}. $$

### D.2 Grad-B tensor in axisymmetry

We first analyze the axisymmetric case relevant to tokamak-like divertors. We employ the standard cylindrical coordinates $(R,\zeta,z)$ with orthonormal vectors $(\bm{\hat{R}}=\bm{\nabla}R,\bm{\hat{\zeta}}=R\bm{\nabla}\zeta,\bm{\hat{z}}=\bm{\nabla}z)$ (D’haeseleer et al., 2012; Freidberg, 2014), and consider a general axisymmetric toroidal magnetic field of the form

$$ \displaystyle\bm{B}=I(\psi)\bm{\nabla}\zeta+\bm{\nabla}\zeta\times\bm{\nabla}\psi,\quad\psi=\psi(R,z). $$

Here, $I(\psi)$ is the current, $\psi(R,z)$ is the poloidal flux surface label that satisfies the Grad-Shafranov equation,

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{,zz}+\psi_{,RR}-\frac{1}{R}\psi_{,R}+R^{2}p^{\prime}(\psi)+II^{\prime}(\psi)=0. $$

The gradient of $\bm{B}$ from (D.6), taking into account

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{\hat{R}}=\frac{\bm{\hat{\zeta}}\bm{\hat{\zeta}}}{R},\quad\bm{\nabla}\bm{\hat{\zeta}}=-\frac{\bm{\hat{\zeta}}\bm{\hat{R}}}{R}, $$

is given by

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}= \displaystyle\frac{1}{R}\left(\bm{\hat{R}}\bm{\nabla}\psi_{,z}-\bm{\hat{z}}\bm{\nabla}\psi_{,R}\right)-\frac{I}{R^{2}}\left(\bm{\hat{\zeta}}\bm{\hat{R}}+\bm{\hat{R}}\bm{\hat{\zeta}}\right) \displaystyle+\left(\frac{I^{\prime}(\psi)}{R}\bm{\nabla}\psi\bm{\hat{\zeta}}-\frac{\bm{\hat{R}}}{R}\frac{\bm{\hat{\zeta}}\times\bm{\nabla}\psi}{R}+\frac{\psi_{,Z}}{R}\frac{\bm{\hat{\zeta}}\bm{\hat{\zeta}}}{R}\right). $$

Near O and X points, where $|\bm{\nabla}\psi|^{2}=(\psi_{,R})^{2}+(\psi_{,z})^{2}\to 0$ , the last term in (D.9) drops out, and $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ takes the simple form

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}=\frac{1}{R}\left(\psi_{,Rz}\left(\bm{\hat{R}}\bm{\hat{R}}-\bm{\hat{z}}\bm{\hat{z}}\right)+\left(\bm{\hat{z}}\bm{\hat{R}}\;\psi_{,zz}-\bm{\hat{R}}\bm{\hat{z}}\;\psi_{,RR}\right)\right)-\frac{I}{R^{2}}\left(\bm{\hat{\zeta}}\bm{\hat{R}}+\bm{\hat{R}}\bm{\hat{\zeta}}\right). $$

In the alternative matrix form in the $(\bm{\hat{\zeta}},\bm{\hat{z}},\bm{\hat{R}})$ basis

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}=\frac{1}{R}\begin{pmatrix}\;\;0\qquad\quad\;0\qquad-I/R\\
\quad 0\qquad-\psi_{,Rz}\qquad\;\psi_{,zz}\\
-I/R\quad-\psi_{,RR}\qquad\psi_{,Rz}\end{pmatrix}, $$

with trace and determinant given by

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{Tr}{\left(\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}\right)}=0,\quad\mbox{Det}{\left(\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}\right)}=\left(\frac{I}{R^{2}}\right)^{2}\psi_{,Rz}. $$

Normalizing the axisymmetric quantities with major radius $R_{a}$ and field strength $B_{a}$ , and denoting normalized quantities by a bar,

$$ \displaystyle\bar{R}=\frac{R}{R_{a}},\quad\overline{z}=\frac{z}{R_{a}},\quad\overline{I}=\frac{I}{B_{a}R_{a}},\quad\overline{\psi}=\frac{\psi}{B_{a}R_{a}^{2}}, $$

we find that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{P}}{(B_{a}/R_{a})^{2}}=\frac{1}{\overline{R}^{2}}\left(\overline{\mathscr{H}}_{2}[\overline{\psi}]-\left(\frac{\overline{I}}{\overline{R}}\right)^{2}\right),\quad\frac{\mathcal{Q}}{(B_{a}/R_{a})^{3}}=-\left(\frac{\overline{I}}{\overline{R}^{2}}\right)^{2}\overline{\psi}_{,\overline{R}\overline{z}}, $$

The normalized eigenvalues $(R_{a}/B_{a})\lambda_{i}$ will be $O(1)$ if $\overline{\mathcal{P}},\overline{\mathcal{Q}}$ are both $O(1)$ .

### D.3 Grad-B tensor near closed field lines

Next, we consider the case of closed field lines, which has been has been discussed extensively by Solov’ev and Shafranov (1970); Mercier (1964); Burby et al. (2021) and others. Avoiding re-derivation, we simply quote relevant formulas from Section 3 and Appendix C of Guinchard et al. (2025). The magnetic axis is assumed to be a smooth curve $\bm{r}_{0}(\ell)$ parametrized by the arclength $\ell$ . A Frenet-Serret frame $(\bm{\hat{t}}(\ell)=\bm{r}_{0}^{\prime}(\ell),\bm{\hat{n}}(\ell),\bm{\hat{b}}(\ell))$ is fitted to the axis such that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d}{d\ell}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{\hat{t}}\\
\bm{\hat{n}}\\
\bm{\hat{b}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\;0\quad+\kappa\quad\;\;0\\
-\kappa\qquad 0\;\;+\tau\\
\;0\quad-\tau\quad\;\;0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{\hat{t}}\\
\bm{\hat{n}}\\
\bm{\hat{b}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Following (Solov’ev and Shafranov, 1970), a set of “rotating frame” $(\bm{\hat{t}},\bm{\mathcal{N}},\bm{\mathcal{B}})$ with a rotation angle $\delta(\ell)$ can then be constructed such that

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\bm{\mathcal{N}}\\
\bm{\mathcal{B}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\delta(\ell)}\quad-\sin{\delta(\ell)}\\
\sin{\delta(\ell)}\quad+\cos{\delta(\ell)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{\hat{n}}\\
\bm{\hat{b}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

The position vector of any point can now be expressed as

$$ \displaystyle\bm{r}=\bm{r}_{0}(\ell)+x\bm{\mathcal{N}}+y\bm{\mathcal{B}}. $$

We obtain the following tangent and the reciprocal basis vectors (D’haeseleer et al., 2012) from (D.17)

$$ \displaystyle\bm{e}_{1}\equiv\partial_{x}\bm{r}=\bm{\mathcal{N}},\quad\bm{e}_{2}\equiv\partial_{y}\bm{r}=\bm{\mathcal{B}},\quad\bm{e}_{3}\equiv\partial_{\ell}\bm{r}=h\bm{\hat{t}}-u^{\prime}(\ell)(x\bm{\mathcal{B}}-y\bm{\mathcal{N}}), \displaystyle\bm{e}^{1}\equiv\bm{\nabla}x=\bm{\mathcal{N}}-\frac{u^{\prime}y}{h}\bm{\hat{t}},\quad\bm{e}^{2}\equiv\bm{\nabla}y=\bm{\mathcal{B}}+\frac{u^{\prime}x}{h}\bm{\hat{t}},\quad\bm{e}^{3}\equiv\bm{\nabla}\ell=\frac{\bm{t}}{h}, \displaystyle\sqrt{g}\equiv\bm{e}_{1}\times\bm{e}_{2}\cdot\bm{e}_{3}=h,\quad h=1-\kappa(x\cos\delta-y\sin{\delta}),\quad u^{\prime}(\ell)=\delta^{\prime}(\ell)-\tau(\ell). $$

To obtain the equation of the field lines and $\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}$ we need $\bm{B}$ in the form

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{g}\bm{B}=\sqrt{g}B^{1}\bm{e}_{1}+\sqrt{g}B^{2}\bm{e}_{2}+\sqrt{g}B^{3}\bm{e}_{3},\quad\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}=B^{3}\partial_{\ell}+B^{1}\partial_{x}+B^{2}\partial_{y}. $$

Analyticity near the closed field line then implies that we can carry out regular Taylor expansions in $(x,y)$

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{g}B^{1}=a_{1}x+a_{2}y,\quad\sqrt{g}B^{2}=b_{1}x+b_{2}y,\quad\sqrt{g}B^{3}=B_{0}+c_{1}x+c_{2}y. $$

Ensuring $\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{B}=0$ , $\bm{\nabla}\times\bm{B}=J_{0}\bm{\hat{t}}$ using (D.21), we get to linear order,

$$ \displaystyle\bm{B}=B_{t}\bm{\hat{t}}+B_{\mathcal{N}}\bm{\mathcal{N}}+B_{\mathcal{B}}\bm{\mathcal{B}}, \displaystyle B_{t}=B_{0}(\ell)+c_{1}x+c_{2}y,\;\;B_{\mathcal{N}}=a_{1}x+(a_{2}+u^{\prime}B_{0})y,\;\;B_{\mathcal{B}}=b_{2}y+(b_{1}-u^{\prime}B_{0})x, \displaystyle\frac{a_{1}}{B_{0}}=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{B_{0}^{\prime}}{B_{0}}+\eta^{\prime}\right),\;\;\frac{b_{2}}{B_{0}}=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{B_{0}^{\prime}}{B_{0}}-\eta^{\prime}\right),\;\;\frac{a_{2}}{B_{0}}=-\Omega_{0}e^{-\eta},\;\;\frac{b_{1}}{B_{0}}=\Omega_{0}e^{\eta}, \displaystyle\frac{c_{1}}{B_{0}}=\kappa\cos\delta,\quad\frac{c_{2}}{B_{0}}=\kappa\sin\delta,\quad\Omega_{0}=\frac{J_{0}/(2B_{0})+u^{\prime}}{\cosh{\eta}},\quad\Omega_{V}=\Omega_{0}\sinh\eta. $$

The flux surface label $\psi=B_{0}(\exp{\eta(\ell)}x^{2}\pm\exp{-\eta(\ell)}y^{2})/2$ is a rotating ellipse or a hyperbola depending on whether we are at an O point or an X point. Whereas $\delta^{\prime}(\ell)$ is the rotation rate of the conic, the elongation is controlled by $\eta^{\prime}$ .

Thus, equation of the field lines and $\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}$ to the lowest order in the distance to the closed field line are

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\ell}{B_{0}}=\frac{dx}{a_{1}x+a_{2}y}=\frac{dy}{b_{1}x+b_{2}y}, \displaystyle\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}=B_{0}\partial_{\ell}+(a_{1}x+a_{2}y)\partial_{x}+(b_{1}x+b_{2}y)\partial_{y}, $$

where $a_{1},b_{1},a_{2},b_{2}$ are given by (D.22).

Finally, the lowest order $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ in the $(\bm{\hat{t}},\bm{\mathcal{N}},\bm{\mathcal{B}})$ basis takes the form

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}=B_{0}\begin{pmatrix}B_{0}^{\prime}/B_{0}\qquad\quad\;\;c_{1}/B_{0}\qquad\qquad c_{2}/B_{0}\quad\\
\qquad c_{1}/B_{0}\qquad\qquad a_{1}/B_{0}\qquad\left(\Omega_{V}+\frac{J_{0}}{2B_{0}}\right)\quad\\
c_{2}/B_{0}\qquad\left(\Omega_{V}-\frac{J_{0}}{2B_{0}}\right)\qquad b_{2}/B_{0}\quad\end{pmatrix}. $$

In the vacuum limit ( $J_{0}=0$ ),

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{,x} \displaystyle=a_{1}x+\Omega_{V}y,\quad\Phi_{,y}=b_{2}y+\Omega_{V}x, \displaystyle\Phi_{,xx} \displaystyle=a_{1},\quad\Phi_{,xy}=\Omega_{V},\quad\Phi_{,yy}=b_{2}, $$

such that the Laplace equation implies $\Phi_{,xx}+\Phi_{,yy}+B_{0}^{\prime}=0$ . The other quantities of interest are given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathscr{H}_{2}[\Phi] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\left(\left(\frac{B_{0}^{\prime}}{B_{0}}\right)^{2}-{\eta^{\prime}}^{2}\right)-\Omega_{V}^{2},\quad\Omega_{V}=\frac{\delta^{\prime}-\tau}{\cosh{\eta}}. \displaystyle-\frac{\mathcal{P}}{B_{0}^{2}} \displaystyle=\left(\kappa^{2}+\frac{\eta^{\prime}}{4}^{2}+\Omega_{V}^{2}\right)+\left(\frac{3B_{0}^{\prime}}{4B_{0}}\right)^{2}, \displaystyle-\frac{\mathcal{Q}}{B_{0}^{3}} \displaystyle=\frac{B_{0}^{\prime}}{B_{0}}\left(\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\left(\left(\frac{B_{0}^{\prime}}{B_{0}}\right)^{2}-{\eta^{\prime}}^{2}\right)-\Omega_{V}^{2}\right)+\kappa^{2}\left(\Omega_{0}\sinh{\eta}\sin{2\delta}-\frac{\eta^{\prime}}{2}\cos{2\delta}\right). $$

The eigenvalues $\lambda_{i}$ normalized to the major radius $R_{a}$ are $O(1)$ , since $\kappa,\tau$ and all $\ell$ derivatives scale as $1/R_{a}$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle R_{a}^{2}\mathscr{H}_{2}[\Phi]\sim\frac{\mathcal{P}}{(B_{0}/R_{a})^{2}}\sim\frac{\mathcal{Q}}{(B_{0}/R_{a})^{3}}\sim O(1)\quad\Rightarrow(R_{a}/B_{0})\lambda_{i}\sim O(1). $$

.

### D.4 Grad-B tensor near ridges

We now focus on generic 3D sharp ridges. We use a local signed Frenet-Serret frame $(\bm{t},\bm{n},\bm{b})$ (D.15) near the ridges together with local coordinates $(\ell,x,y)$ . We orient the signed Frenet frame such that the tangent vector $\bm{t}$ is aligned with the ridge, which is assumed to be a smooth space curve. The arclength along the ridge is measured by $\ell$ . Since we expect the field line curvature and torsion to vanish exactly on the ridge, we choose the normal $\bm{n}$ and therefore the binormal $\bm{b}=\bm{t}\times\bm{n}$ directions such that continuity is maintained in the vicinity of the ridge. The distances along normal and binormal is measured by local variables $x$ and $y$ . Thus, we can define the position vector as

$$ \displaystyle\bm{r}=\bm{r}_{0}(\ell)+x\bm{\hat{n}}(\ell)+y\bm{\hat{b}}(\ell). $$

Upon differentiation (D.28) yields the following tangent basic vectors (D’haeseleer et al., 2012)

$$ \displaystyle\bm{e}_{1}\equiv\partial_{x}\bm{r}=\bm{\hat{n}},\quad\bm{e}_{2}\equiv\partial_{y}\bm{r}=\bm{\hat{b}},\quad\bm{e}_{3}\equiv\partial_{\ell}\bm{r}=h\bm{\hat{t}}+\tau(x\bm{b}-y\bm{n}), $$

where $h$ is the Jacobian

$$ \displaystyle h\equiv\bm{e}_{1}\times\bm{e}_{2}\cdot\bm{e}_{3}=1-\kappa x. $$

The reciprocal basis vectors, given by

$$ \displaystyle\bm{e}^{1}\equiv\bm{\nabla}x=\bm{\hat{n}}+\frac{\tau y}{h}\bm{\hat{t}},\quad\bm{e}^{2}\equiv\bm{\nabla}y=\bm{\hat{b}}-\frac{\tau x}{h}\bm{\hat{t}},\quad\bm{e}^{3}\equiv\bm{\nabla}\ell=\frac{\bm{t}}{h}. $$

The set-up so far is identical to the closed field line case D.3 with $\delta=0$ . However, the key difference is that a regular Taylor series is not warranted near the ridges. However, we can still define a $B_{0}(\ell)$ analogous to the closed field line case by defining $B_{0}\equiv B_{t}(x=0,y=0,\ell)$ . In the following, we restrict ourselves to vacuum fields $\bm{B}=\bm{\nabla}\Phi$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\bm{B} \displaystyle=B_{t}\bm{\hat{t}}+B_{n}\bm{\hat{n}}+B_{b}\bm{\hat{b}}, \displaystyle B_{t} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{h}\left(\Phi_{,\ell}+\tau\left(y\Phi_{,x}-x\Phi_{,y}\right)\right),\quad B_{n}=\Phi_{,x},\quad B_{b}=\Phi_{,y}. \displaystyle\sqrt{g}B^{1} \displaystyle=h\bm{B}\cdot\bm{e}^{1}=hB_{n}+\tau yB_{t},\;\;\sqrt{g}B^{2}=hB_{b}-\tau xB_{t},\;\;\sqrt{g}B^{3}=B_{t}. $$

Thus, equation of the field lines and $\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}$ to the lowest order in the distance to the closed field line are

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\ell}{B_{0}}=\frac{dx}{\Phi_{,x}+B_{0}\tau y}=\frac{dy}{\Phi_{,y}-B_{0}\tau x}, \displaystyle\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}=B_{0}\partial_{\ell}+(\Phi_{,x}+B_{0}\tau y)\partial_{x}+(\Phi_{,y}-B_{0}\tau x)\partial_{y}, $$

Implementing the same procedure as in the closed field line case, we find the following form for the lowest order $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ in the $(\bm{\hat{t}},\bm{\hat{n}},\bm{\hat{b}})$ basis

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}=\begin{pmatrix}B_{0}^{\prime}\qquad\kappa B_{0}\qquad\quad 0\;\;\\
\;\;\kappa B_{0}\qquad\Phi_{,xx}\qquad\Phi_{,xy}\;\;\\
\quad 0\qquad\;\;\;\Phi_{,xy}\qquad\;\Phi_{,yy}\;\;\end{pmatrix}. $$

The quantities $\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q}$ from (D.34) are

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{\mathcal{P}}{B_{0}^{2}}=\kappa^{2}+\left(\frac{B_{0}^{\prime}}{B_{0}}\right)^{2}-\mathscr{H}_{2}[\varphi],\quad-\frac{\mathcal{Q}}{B_{0}^{3}}=\frac{B_{0}^{\prime}}{B_{0}}\mathscr{H}_{2}[\varphi]-\kappa^{2}\varphi_{,yy},\quad\varphi=\frac{\Phi}{B_{0}}. $$

Near the ridges, $B_{0}^{\prime}\to 0,\kappa\to 0$ . Thus, $\mathcal{Q}\to 0,\mathcal{P}/B_{0}^{2}\to\mathscr{H}_{2}[\varphi]$ . Now, if $R_{a}^{2}\mathscr{H}_{2}[\varphi]\sim O(1)$ , $R_{a}\lambda_{i}\sim O(1)$ . However, we showed $\mathscr{H}_{2}=K_{G}$ , which can be very large. Thus, normalized eigenvalues are not necessarily $O(1)$ .

## Appendix E Expansion of the Biot-Savart expression near a filamentary coil

It is convenient to use the orthogonal Mercier coordinate system $(\rho,\omega,\ell)$ (Mercier, 1964; Solov’ev and Shafranov, 1970; Sengupta et al., 2021; Jorge et al., 2020b), which is exactly what Callegari and Ting (1978) used to carry out the local induction approximation (LIA) without explicitly calling it the Mercier coordinates.

Starting with the current filament defined by the space curve $\bm{r}_{0}(\ell)$ parameterized by the arclength $\ell$ , we construct an orthonormal Frenet-Serret frame $(\bm{\hat{t}}(\ell)=\bm{r}_{0}^{\prime}(\ell),\bm{\hat{n}}(\ell),\bm{\hat{b}}(\ell))$ that satisfies the frame equations (D.15) with curvature and torsion given by $\kappa_{c},\tau_{c}$ . Here, the subscript $c$ will be used to denote coil filaments.

Next, we define a position vector $\bm{r}=\bm{r}_{0}(\ell)+\rho\bm{\hat{\rho}}$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\hat{\rho}} \displaystyle=\bm{\hat{n}}\cos\theta+\bm{\hat{b}}\sin\theta,\quad\bm{\hat{\omega}}=-\bm{\hat{n}}\sin\theta+\bm{\hat{b}}\cos\theta,\quad\cos{\theta}=\bm{\bm{\hat{n}}}\cdot\bm{\hat{\rho}},\quad\omega=\theta+\int\tau d\ell, \displaystyle\partial_{\rho}\bm{r} \displaystyle=\bm{\hat{\rho}},\quad\partial_{\omega}\bm{r}=\rho\;\bm{\hat{\omega}},\quad\partial_{\ell}\bm{r}=h\bm{\bm{\hat{t}}},\quad h\equiv 1-\kappa\rho\cos\theta, \displaystyle\partial_{\ell}\bm{\hat{\rho}} \displaystyle=-\kappa\cos\theta\bm{\hat{t}},\quad\partial_{\ell}\bm{\hat{\omega}}=\kappa\sin\theta\bm{\hat{t}}. $$

In addition we can show that

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{\hat{\rho}}=\frac{1}{\rho}\bm{\hat{\omega}}\bm{\hat{\omega}}-\frac{\kappa\cos\theta}{h}\bm{\hat{t}}\bm{\hat{t}},\;\;\bm{\nabla}\bm{\hat{\omega}}=-\frac{1}{\rho}\bm{\hat{\omega}}\bm{\hat{\rho}}+\frac{\kappa\sin\theta}{h}\bm{\hat{t}}\bm{\hat{t}},\;\;\bm{\nabla}\bm{\hat{t}}=\frac{\kappa}{h}\bm{\hat{t}}\bm{\hat{n}}. $$

From $\bm{B}=B_{\rho}\bm{\hat{\rho}}+B_{\omega}\bm{\hat{\omega}}+O(\rho)$ , with both $B_{\rho},B_{\omega}$ having $1/\rho,\ln{\rho}$ terms, we find that $\partial_{\ell}B_{\rho},\partial_{\ell}B_{\omega}$ are $O(\rho)$ smaller compared to terms such as $\partial_{\rho}B_{\rho},(1/\rho)\partial_{\omega}B_{\rho}$ . Thus, we naturally end up with

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}=\centering\begin{pmatrix}-\kappa_{c}B_{n}\qquad\qquad 0\qquad\qquad\qquad 0\qquad\\
0\qquad\qquad\partial_{\rho}B_{\rho}\qquad\qquad\partial_{\rho}B_{\omega}\\
\qquad\quad 0\qquad\frac{1}{\rho}(-B_{\omega}+\partial_{\omega}B_{\rho})\quad\frac{1}{\rho}(B_{\rho}+\partial_{\omega}B_{\omega})\end{pmatrix},\@add@centering $$

where

$$ \displaystyle B_{n}\equiv\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\hat{n}}=B_{\rho}\cos\theta-B_{\omega}\sin\theta. $$

We now define a reduced determinant surface $\mathscr{D}=0$ corresponding to $B_{n}=0$ . This surface can be given a natural interpretation of an effective flux surface such that the normal component of $\bm{B}$ given by $B_{n}$ vanishes on the surface. Thus, it is natural to parametrize the determinant $\mathscr{D}=0$ by

$$ \displaystyle\bm{r}=\bm{r}_{0}(\ell)+\rho_{\mathscr{D}}\bm{\hat{n}}. $$

We have the following tangent vectors on the determinant surface

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\rho_{\mathscr{D}}}\bm{r}=\bm{\hat{n}},\quad\partial_{\ell}\bm{r}=h_{c}\bm{\hat{t}}+\rho_{\mathscr{D}}\tau_{c}\bm{\hat{b}},\quad h_{c}=1-\kappa_{c}\rho_{\mathscr{D}}\cos\theta. $$

In the limit of $\rho_{\mathscr{D}}\to 0$ , the tangent vectors are $\bm{\hat{n}}$ and $\bm{\hat{t}}$ The unit normal vector to the determinant surface is

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\bm{N}}=\frac{\partial_{\ell}\bm{r}\times\partial_{\rho_{\mathscr{D}}}\bm{r}}{|\partial_{\ell}\bm{r}\times\partial_{\rho_{\mathscr{D}}}\bm{r}|}=\bm{\hat{b}} $$

Thus, the binormal vector $\bm{\hat{b}}$ is the normal to the surface $\hat{\bm{N}}$ , which is a textbook (Struik, 2012) example of asymptotic curves on a ruled surface. For asymptotic curves Gaussian curvature is non-positive and can be related to the torsion through $K_{G\mathscr{D}}=-\tau_{c}^{2}$ .

Finally, for the sake of rigor, we now define a normalized determinant $\bar{\mathscr{D}}_{3}$ that stays finite as we approach the Det $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ surface. The essential idea is to use the Cayley - Hamilton invariants for a traceless symmetric matrix such as $\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ . As discussed in Appendix D, the characteristic equation Det $(\lambda\mathbb{I}-\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})$ leads to the invariants $\mathcal{P}=-(1/2)\text{Tr}((\bm{\nabla}\bm{B})^{2})$ and $\mathcal{Q}=-\text{Det}\bm{\nabla}\bm{B}$ . In terms of the three real eigenvalues $(\lambda_{0},\lambda_{\pm})$ , $\mathcal{P}=(-1/2)(\lambda_{0}^{2}+\lambda_{+}^{2}+\lambda_{-}^{2}),\mathcal{Q}=-\lambda_{0}\lambda_{+}\lambda_{-}$ . As we approach the current filament, $\lambda_{0}\to 0$ while $\lambda_{\pm}$ blow up. In this limit $\lambda_{-}\to-\lambda_{+}$ , such that $-\mathcal{P}\to\lambda_{+}^{2},\mathcal{Q}\to\lambda_{0}\lambda_{+}^{2}$ . To isolate the null eigenvalue surface defined by $\lambda_{0}$ , we now define $\bar{\mathscr{D}}_{3}{}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\bar{\mathscr{D}}_{3}{}\equiv\frac{\mathcal{Q}}{(-\mathcal{P})^{3/2}}. $$

The $3/2$ power ensures a smooth continuity $\bar{\mathscr{D}}_{3}{}\to 0$ as we take the limit $\rho\to 0$ . Other choices are also possible, but we do not dwell on that here. The normalized determinant is useful for numerical purposes as it is designed to be smooth near coils. However, it does not change the conclusions obtained from $\mathscr{D}_{3}\to 0$ . The reason is that $\mathscr{D}_{3}\to 0$ not because of any power of $\rho$ but because of the $\sin\theta$ factor that goes to zero near the coils.

# Periodic Korteweg-de Vries soliton potentials generate quasisymmetric magnetic fields

## Abstract

Quasisymmetry (QS) is a hidden symmetry of the magnetic field strength, $B=|{\bm{B}}|$ , that effectively confines charged particles in a three-dimensional toroidal plasma equilibrium. Here, we show that QS has a deep connection to the underlying symmetry that makes solitons possible. Our approach uncovers a hidden lower dimensionality of $B$ on a magnetic flux surface, which could make stellarator optimization schemes significantly more efficient. Recent numerical breakthroughs (M. Landreman and E. Paul, Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 035001 (2022)) have yielded configurations with excellent volumetric QS and surprisingly low magnetic shear. Given $B$ , it may be possible to deduce an upper bound on the maximum quasisymmetric toroidal volume which depends only on the properties of $B$ . This has been verified for the Landreman-Paul precise quasiaxisymmetric (QA) stellarator configuration. In the neighborhood of the outermost surface, we show that $B$ approaches the form of the 1-soliton reflectionless potential (I. Gjaja and A. Bhattacharjee, Phys. Rev. Lett. 68, 2413 (1992)). The connection length diverges, indicating the possible presence of an X-point or cusp that could potentially be used as a basis for a divertor. We present a non-perturbative approach based on ensuring single-valuedness of $B$ , which directly leads to its Painlevé property and the KdV and Gardner’s equations. Finally, we use an approach based on machine learning, trained on a large dataset of numerically optimized quasisymmetric stellarators. We robustly recover the KdV and Gardner’s equations from the data.

## I Introduction

Physical systems possessing a hidden symmetry attract serious attention [20, 52, 54, 48, 57, 51] because of the far-reaching impact of the symmetry on the physical properties of the systems. The hidden symmetry manifests only in special coordinates, which are constructed, along with the invariants, as part of the solution to the problem. In the presence of hidden symmetries, the partial differential equations (PDEs) governing classical dynamical fields often reduce to integrable PDEs [57, 60, 51]. An example of the latter is the well-known Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation with soliton solutions [30, 59].

In plasma physics, a hidden symmetry called quasisymmetry (QS)[9, 37], forces the time-independent magnetic field strength, $B=|\bm{B}|$ , to be symmetric [9, 72], whereas the full vector magnetic field $\bm{B}$ itself depends on all three spatial coordinates, and is thus said to be three-dimensional (3D). The similarity of this symmetry to particle relabelling symmetries [62, 83] is known [72, 85] but yet to be fully explored.

The hidden symmetry in $B$ makes the bounce action (second adiabatic invariant), $J_{\|}$ , independent of the field-line label [37], which guarantees excellent particle confinement in a torus. The 3D nature of B allows stellarators enough flexibility to avoid intrinsic difficulties (such as powerful transients) associated with large plasma currents in axisymmetric configurations such as tokamaks.

It is currently unknown whether exact QS can be achieved in a toroidal volume for a magnetic field that satisfies the constraint of force balance in ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) [28]. The problem is of fundamental importance and potentially significant for the design of next-generation stellarator fusion reactors. Analytical results [32, 31, 64, 50] seem to indicate that in the presence of scalar plasma pressure, the resulting 3D nonlinear system of PDEs does not have solutions in a toroidal volume [32, 31, 50, 22, 69, 70]. In particular, the near-axis expansion (NAE), which is an asymptotic expansion in the distance from the magnetic axis [55, 80, 6], when applied to QS [32, 31, 49], becomes overdetermined beyond the second order. Moreover, NAEs are typically divergent [29] beyond second order.

Overdetermined problems do not generally have solutions. Even when they have solutions, they may still be subject to restrictive constraints. For example, in the particular case of isodynamic magnetic fields, which satisfy a constraint more restrictive than QS [37, 76], it has been shown [63, 76] that if a solution exists, it must be essentially 2D: either axisymmetric like a tokamak or a helically symmetric straight stellarator.

On the other hand, numerical 3D toroidal stellarator solutions with a precise level of QS and MHD force balance have been obtained via numerical optimization, suggesting the existence of special, physically interesting toroidal solutions to the overdetermined problem. However, the numerical search over a typically vast parameter space obscures insight into the quasisymmetric configuration space that permits precise solutions. In particular, optimized quasisymmetric configurations tend to form clusters in parameter space [68, 33], and may be due to a hidden lower-dimensionality that warrants further analysis.

To construct an analytical model of quasisymmetric vacuum fields in a generic non-symmetric toroidal domain, we must first discuss the fundamental requirements of such a theory. First and foremost, we require global toroidal solutions for $B$ that respect double periodicity (both poloidal and toroidal). We restrict ourselves to the class of smooth magnetic fields that are assumed to be analytic. The analyticity requirement can be rigorously justified near the axis [32, 49, 79]. Our analyticity requirement currently excludes interesting classes such as piecewise omnigeneous stellarators [82], which can have sharp changes in the gradients of the field strength.

Second, we require field-line independence of $J_{\|}$ , as part of the definition of the properties of QS and omnigeneity. The connection with the KdV equation comes from identifying the field-line label $\alpha$ as time. With this identification, we further require that the adiabatic invariant $J_{\|}$ be an exact (time-independent) invariant. Most adiabatic invariants with analytic time-dependent potentials are not exact. For example, it can be shown that over a long time, adiabatic invariants change by [46, 38] equal to $C\exp{(-1/\epsilon)}$ , where $C$ is a positive $\epsilon$ -dependent constant where $\epsilon\ll 1$ is the slowness or the adiabatic parameter. Fortunately, there exist privileged time-dependent potentials for which the coefficient $C$ multiplying the exponentially small term vanishes identically. Consequently, the adiabatic invariants become exact invariants [35, 7]. Since $C$ is proportional to the reflection coefficient in the case of above-barrier reflection from a potential well [44, 35, 7], such potentials are also called reflectionless potentials. Reflectionless potentials are intimately connected with solitons and integrable systems [3, 59] where they naturally appear in the long wavelength limit of periodic cnoidal waves.

Broadening the search to other integrable periodic nonlinear waves leads us to the question, posed by R.S. MacKay, as to whether Painlevé analysis could determine non-axisymmetric QS equilibrium 11 1 R. MacKay, private communication (Simons team meeting 2019, The Painlevé property (PP) should perhaps also be referred to as the Kovalevskaya-Painlevé property since Kovalevskaya used it to find new cases of integrable tops before Painlevé’s work was published (Michéle Audin, Spinning tops: A course on integrable systems, Vol. 51 (Cambridge University Press, 1999)).. The Painlevé analysis, which involves the study of singularities of differential equations in the complex domain, has yielded fundamental results in several physics problems from quantum field theory to optics [53]. Analytic continuation from the real to the complex plane is a helpful technique that physicists often utilize in solving linear problems. For nonlinear systems, Kovaleskaya showed that continuation to the complex plane and analyzing singularities can be equally insightful. Moreover, singularities in the complex plane, even those that are far from the real line, can determine and control the behavior of analytic functions on the real line. An important example of this is the doubly periodic elliptic function [39, 86] for which, singularities determine its periodicity on the real line.

In our context, the Painlevé analysis offers a useful methodology for ensuring global analyticity and single-valuedness of the quasisymmetric solutions in the toroidal domain, which is a highly nontrivial problem. The Painlevé property, shared by reflectionless and soliton potentials such as cnoidal waves, guarantees robust exact invariants, global analyticity, and the single-valuedness of $B$ in a toroidal domain. Although it is a priori not obvious that quasisymmetric $B$ belongs to such a restricted class of potentials, the cnoidal solution is entirely consistent with the NAE approach within its limit of applicability.

In this work, we demonstrate that QS admits a class of analytic $B$ that is a periodic solution [59, 42] of the KdV equation. Starting from the basic definitions and properties of QS and requiring only the analyticity and single-valuedness of $B$ , we show, non-perturbatively, the connection to the theory of periodic KdV solitons. In making the connection to soliton theory, we demonstrate how the field-line label independence of the second adiabatic invariant $J_{\|}$ and other integrals of $B$ in QS are directly related to the infinite hierarchy of conserved quantities of the KdV equation. The exact analytic solution for $B$ is valid in the entire toroidal volume and reduces to the NAE predictions close to the axis.

Our final approach is data-driven. We use PySINDy [24, 43] to look for relations between $B$ and its derivatives in the large family of quasi-axisymmetric configurations generated in [15] and the QUASR database [34]. PySINDy employs sparse regression techniques and algorithms to discover governing dynamical system models from noisy, limited data. We show that, over a wide range of configurations and parameters, the KdV equation with the traveling-wave form for $B$ holds. As described later in the paper, the only exceptions we found are covered by Gardner’s equation.

The connection with periodic KdV solitons allows us to describe $B$ on a magnetic flux surface with only three functions of the magnetic flux, which are related to the so-called spectral parameters [59] of the KdV equation. We show that these functions are closely related to the spectrum of $B$ in Boozer coordinates [37] where the hidden symmetry is manifest, thereby highlighting the low dimensionality of the Boozer spectrum. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the periodicity of $B$ is maintained only when these functions are distinct. Consequently, it may be possible to estimate the region of validity of volumetric QS based on where the two spectral parameters intersect (discussed below). Remarkably, near the point of intersection, the connection length (period of $B$ ) begins to diverge, and $B$ approaches the form of a reflectionless potential (a single soliton that decays at infinity) [35, 7]. The diverging connection length is a characteristic of an X-point or sharp ridge that could potentially be the basis for a non-resonant divertor [56, 10, 67].

We demonstrate, using both data-driven and traditional numerical methods, that our analytic theory can describe well the properties of the field strength on a flux surface of the vacuum equilibrium with precise quasi-axisymmetry (QA) [48] and some other optimized quasisymmetric configurations as well.

## II Basic formulation of quasisymmetry

We begin by reviewing some of the known basic properties of QS. Several equivalent [37, 72, 28, 16, 69] mathematical descriptions of QS exist. In this Section, we briefly discuss the most relevant equations and coordinates to describe QS and point out their inter-relationships. Here and throughout the paper, we assume the existence of a set of nested toroidal magnetic surfaces, of the kind illustrated in Fig. 1. These assumptions are standard within magnetic confinement theory. For details about the coordinates, see for example Ref. [26].

*Figure 1: An illustration of a toroidal surface with toroidal angle ( $\Phi$ ), poloidal angle ( $\theta$ ) and flux-surface label $\psi$ . Figure adapted from Ref. [40].*

It can be shown that QS implies the existence of a divergence-free vector field $\bm{u}$ that satisfies the system [69]

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{u} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\bm{B}\times\bm{u} \displaystyle=\bm{\nabla}\psi. $$

In (1c), $\psi$ can be any flux function (i.e. any single-valued function that satisfies $\vec{B}\cdot\nabla\psi=0$ ). It follows directly from (1c) and the divergence-free nature of $\bm{u},\bm{B}$ that $\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}$ and $\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}$ commute, i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle[\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla},\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}]=0. $$

Here, we have used the usual definition of the commutator $[A_{1},A_{2}]\equiv A_{1}A_{2}-A_{2}A_{1}$ for two operators $A_{1},A_{2}$ .

The mathematical structure of (1) strongly suggests that $\bm{u}$ can be associated with a particle-relabelling symmetry group ([62, 61, 73, 74, 84, 83] and references therein) with density replaced by the field strength [72, 85]. Therefore, understanding the hidden symmetry underlying QS might also be beneficial in understanding Casimirs [36, 62] in ideal MHD and hydrodynamics.

From equation (1c) it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\bm{u}=(F(\psi)\bm{B}-\bm{B}\times\bm{\nabla}\psi)/B^{2}. $$

The condition (1b) then implies

$$ \displaystyle\bm{B}\times\bm{\nabla}\psi\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=F(\psi)\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B, $$

which is sometimes called the two-term form of QS [69].

For a vacuum field $\bm{B}=G_{0}\bm{\nabla}\Phi$ [8, 37],

$$ \displaystyle F(\psi)=G_{0}q_{N},\quad q_{N}\equiv(\iota-N)^{-1}, $$

where $\iota$ is the rotational transform, $N$ is the helicity of QS, $2\pi G_{0}/\mu_{0}$ is the poloidal current outside the surface and $\Phi$ is a toroidal angle. Moreover, the two-term form of QS (equivalently $\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=0$ ) for vacuum fields leads to a traveling wave (TW) solution for $B$ [78] of the form

$$ \displaystyle|\bm{B}|=B(\Phi+(F(\psi)/G_{0})\alpha,\psi),\quad F(\psi)/G_{0}=q_{N}. $$

Thus, the rotational transform and, hence, the magnetic shear enters the definition of QS (4) in a fundamental way. Furthermore, the TW form of $B$ indicates that in the Boozer coordinate system $(\psi,\vartheta_{B},\phi_{B})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{B}=\Phi,\quad\vartheta_{B}=\alpha+(\iota-N)\Phi,\quad|\bm{B}|=B(\vartheta_{B},\psi), $$

i.e., the field strength $B$ depends only on a single angle $\vartheta_{B}$ . Thus, QS manifests itself in these coordinates. This is true not just for the vacuum field but also in the presence of currents and finite pressure in the plasma.

Another form of QS is the so-called “triple-product” form [72, 69]

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\nabla}\psi\times\bm{\nabla}B\cdot\bm{\nabla}\left(\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B\right)=0. $$

The two-term and the triple-product form of QS are equivalent under the assumption of irrational $\iota$ and continuity on rational surfaces [37]. Alternatively, the form

$$ \displaystyle\bm{u}=(\bm{\nabla}\psi\times\bm{\nabla}B)/\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B, $$

is consistent with (3), satisfies (1b), (1c), while (1a) implies (8).

It is useful to use the standard Clebsch coordinate system [37, 26] , $(\psi,\alpha,\ell)$ , such that $\bm{B}=\bm{\nabla}\psi\times\bm{\nabla}\alpha$ with flux label $\psi$ , field-line label $\alpha$ , and $\ell$ , the arclength along the magnetic field. We impose suitable toroidal cuts since $\alpha$ is a multi-valued function. The triple-product form (8) now reads [28]

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial B}{\partial\ell}=f(B,\psi). $$

where $f$ is an arbitrary function of $\psi$ and $B$ . Note that the relation is only valid locally. For $B$ with only one magnetic well, it suffices to introduce branchs cut at the extrema of $B(\ell)$ , which effectively makes $f$ depend on $\sigma=\text{sign}(\partial_{\ell}B)$ as an additional parameter.

In toroidal geometry, $B$ is subject to the following periodic boundary condition [37]:

$$ \displaystyle B(\psi,\alpha,\ell)=B(\psi,\alpha,\ell+L(\psi)). $$

The period of $B$ , $L(\psi)$ , is called the connection length and is a quantity of great physical interest [5].

As shown in Appendix A, in $(\psi,\alpha,\ell)$ coordinates, the $\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=0$ condition takes the form [28]

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\alpha}B+H(\psi,\alpha)\partial_{\ell}B=0, $$

where $H(\psi,\alpha)$ is independent of $\ell$ and depends on the definition of the origin of $\ell$ . It follows from (12) that

$$ \displaystyle H(\psi,\alpha)=-\frac{\left.\partial_{\alpha}B\right|_{\ell}}{\left.\partial_{\ell}B\right|_{\alpha}}=\left.\left(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\alpha}\right)\right|_{B} $$

We note that there is a degree of freedom in choosing the $(\ell,\alpha)$ pair. By transforming to the coordinates $(\overline{\ell},\alpha)$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\ell}\equiv\ell-\int H(\psi,\alpha)d\alpha, $$

we find that

$$ \displaystyle\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}=-\left.\partial_{\alpha}\right|_{\overline{\ell}},\;\;\bm{B}\cdot\bm{\nabla}=B\partial_{\overline{\ell}},\;\; $$

The condition (12) then reduces to

$$ \displaystyle\left.\partial_{\alpha}\right|_{\overline{\ell}}B=0\quad\text{i.e.}\quad B=B(\overline{\ell},\psi). $$

Thus, there exists a special TW frame ( $\overline{\ell},\alpha$ ) for QS where the field strength $B$ is independent of $\alpha$ [28]. We show the equivalence of the two TW forms of $B$ given by (7) and (16) in Appendix B.

There are, in addition, important integral constraints that follow from the requirements of QS. From the $\partial_{\ell}B$ condition (10), any integral along the magnetic field line between two points of equal values of $B=B_{b}$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\alpha}\int_{B\leq B_{b}}d\ell\;F(B;\psi)=0. $$

The field-line independence of the second adiabatic invariant $J_{\|}$

$$ \displaystyle J_{\|}=\oint\sqrt{\mathcal{E}-B}\;d\ell, $$

where $\mathcal{E}$ is related to the particle energy, is a special case of (17). It follows from (17) that quasisymmetric $B$ cannot have local maxima or minima on a flux surface [37, 47].

The distinctions between the cases of exact symmetry (axisymmetry or helical symmetry in a straight cylinder), QS and omnigeneity must now be made clear. For the special cases of exact symmetry, the equations (1) can be solved by letting $u$ be a Killing vector of Euclidean space [16], which decouples $\bm{u}$ from $\bm{B}$ such that $\bm{B}$ is determined by $\bm{u}$ . In other words, $u$ is given by the symmetry of the underlying space and does not need to be solved for. Therefore, the condition (1b), $\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=0$ , can be trivially satisfied. Here, we focus on the case of 3D QS where $\bm{u}$ cannot be posited a priori. Consequently, the condition (1b) imposes a nontrivial constraint. In particular, unlike the case of exact symmetry, the functional form of $f(B,\psi)$ in the $\partial_{\ell}B$ equation must be constrained. We address this question directly in this work.

QS being a special case of omnigeneity [37], the integral property (17) also holds for omnigeneous magnetic fields. However, significant differences arise because omnigeneity is not a local property, and a symmetry vector $\bm{u}$ does not exist in general for omnigeneous magnetic fields. Thus, the local conditions such as (4) or (10), which follow from the properties of $\bm{u}$ do not hold for omnigeneity. It follows that omnigenous fields need not be of the TW form (6). Furthermore, unlike QS [32, 49], omnigeneous $B$ need not be uniformly analytic on a flux surface [17, 18, 65].

As a final step, one must impose a force-balance condition. Without imposing force balance, one can satisfy the QS condition exactly order by order in the NAE [70]. However, the nonlinear overdetermination problem that results when the force-balance condition is imposed is severely restrictive [32, 31] and analytically prohibitive beyond standard near-axis expansions. This will be addressed in future work.

## III The connection of QS to integrable PDEs: Painlevé property

In this Section, we take a non-perturbative route to show that the QS-KdV connection can be established using only three fundamental properties of $B$ as discussed in Section II. First, physical quantities such as $B,\psi$ are assumed to be analytic and single-valued functions of their arguments. Second, $B$ must satisfy the periodic boundary condition (11) in $\ell$ on a flux surface with a period $L(\psi)$ . Third, $\bm{u}$ must be such that a nontrivial special frame exists where $B$ is $\alpha$ independent.

We note that the first assumption is physically reasonable, has been shown to hold near the axis [32], and is also borne out by extensive computations. The second assumption is an essential requirement for QS. (None of the three assumptions hold for omnigeneity.) Regarding the third assumption, an alternative is to demand that $B$ must satisfy the fundamental TW condition (6) everywhere on the flux surface. The third condition leads to an infinite number of field-line $\alpha$ -independent integrals of the form (17).

Before we proceed with our analysis, let us discuss some of the important known exceptional cases of QS. As stated earlier, the case with an exact symmetry is a special case of QS because $\bm{u}$ is determined independently of $\bm{B}$ . Therefore, the third condition $\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=0$ is satisfied identically for every choice of $f(B,\psi)$ in the $\partial_{\ell}B$ equation (10). We find a similar degeneracy in approximate QS near axisymmetry [77, 64, 66], where no constraints exist on $\partial_{\ell}B$ . A more general analysis shows that in configurations that are not close to either axisymmetry or helical symmetry, the degeneracy is avoided, and $\partial_{\ell}B$ is once again constrained [58]. We shall also exclude the exceptional case of zero rotational transform [75] since we focus only on irrational surfaces while assuming continuity on rational surfaces. We shall return to the comparison with the axisymmetric case at the end of this Section.

Our main goal is to study the single-valuedness of $B$ on a constant flux surface $\psi$ that satisfies the $\partial_{\ell}B$ equation (10) and the $\partial_{\alpha}B$ equation (12), subject to the periodicity condition (11).

We first shift to the TW frame where $B$ is $\alpha$ independent, and the $\partial_{\ell}B$ equation can be treated as an ordinary differential equation (ODE) in $\ell$ with period $L(\psi)$ . Since $B$ is assumed to be a real analytic function of $\ell$ on the real interval $(0,L)$ with a nonzero radius of convergence, we can extend it to a complex analytic function $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{Z})$ inside the disk $|\mathcal{Z}|<L$ with $\mathcal{Z}$ denoting the complex $\ell$ . To be precise, we shall now demand that $\mathcal{B}$ be a single-valued complex function of $\mathcal{Z}$ , such that it has the same value at every point independent of the path along which it is reached by analytic continuation.

To proceed further, we need critical ideas from the well-developed theory of complex ODEs [41, 39, 23]. In contrast to solutions of linear ODEs, whose singularities are determined by those of the coefficients, nonlinear ODEs allow movable singularities, which depend on the initial conditions. The standard example is $y^{\prime}+y^{2}=0$ , whose general solution, $y=(x-x_{0})^{-1}$ , depends on the integration constant $x_{0}$ determined by the initial condition $y(0)=-x_{0}^{-1}$ . The possible singularities of ODEs are known. They include poles, branch points, essential singular points, and essential singular lines. Single-valuedness of functions breaks down near critical singularities, such as branch points of algebraic or logarithmic nature. If the critical singularities are fixed, the functions can be made single-valued by defining suitable branch cuts or fixed Riemann surfaces. However, the presence of singularities, which are both critical and movable, leads to dense multi-valuedness around movable singularities of solutions and nonintegrability ([23, 45] and references therein). The absence of movable critical singularities in the general solution of an ODE is called the Painlevé property (PP) of an ODE.

We now look for $\mathcal{B}$ with the PP such that there are no critical singularities in the entire complex plane since their very presence can affect $\mathcal{B}$ on the real line. We now recall some classical results on ODEs with the PP (details given in [41, 39, 23]). Let us rewrite the $\partial_{\ell}B$ equation in the complex plane as a first-order ODE

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}^{\prime}(\mathcal{Z})=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{Z})). $$

The classification of the ODEs according to the PP depends on the degree of the ODE, or equivalently the algebraic power of the $\mathcal{B}^{\prime}(\mathcal{Z})$ . The only first-order ODE of the first degree that possesses the PP is the Riccati equation, where $\mathcal{F}$ is quadratic in $\mathcal{B}$ .

For first-order ODEs of degree $n>1$ , the equations of the form

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}^{\prime}(\mathcal{Z})^{n}=P_{m}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{Z})) $$

with $P_{m}$ a polynomial of degree $m$ , possess the PP provided $n\leq 2m$ . Furthermore, only four possibilities exhaust all ODEs of the form (20). With suitable variable transformations, all of them can be reduced to the following ODE with a cubic nonlinearity

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}^{\prime}(\mathcal{Z})^{2}=P_{3}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{Z})), $$

which is exactly solvable in terms of elliptic functions and their degenerate cases. As is well-known, elliptic functions are doubly-periodic, meromorphic functions. The dependence on the arbitrary initial condition or the TW frame thus leads to only movable poles and no movable critical singularities. Hence, the solution possesses the PP. These classical results follow from the standard Painlevé test and extensions of Malmquist’s theorem [39, 27]. They show how stringent and rigid the constraint of single-valuedness can be.

Returning to the QS problem, we first observe that the Riccati equation for $B$ is inconsistent with the NAE solution. The Riccati equation for $B$ has constant real coefficients on a flux surface, which does not admit nontrivial periodic solutions on the real line [21]. For degrees $n>1$ , the periodicity condition can be easily satisfied with the elliptic functions for the cubic and quartic cases. Now, the cubic and quartic polynomials are the twice-integrated forms of the KdV and Gardner’s equations. The PP of the KdV and Gardner’s equation in the TW frame is well-known and is conjectured to be essential for integrable PDEs with soliton solutions [1, 2].

We now address the question: is the PP necessary and sufficient for a quasisymmetric $B$ ? It is certainly sufficient for QS since both the triple product form (8) and the periodicity condition can be satisfied. However, the necessity is not apparent, particularly in light of axisymmetry, where no such stringent restriction on $\partial_{\ell}B$ appears. In axisymmetry, weak singularities such as $R^{m}\log{R}^{n}$ , with integer $m,n$ , often arise in the description of $\psi$ [19] and in $B$ in cylindrical coordinates. However, these singularities are fixed and, therefore, not of the critical movable type. To further understand the difference between a perfectly axisymmetric system and a system with excellent but not exact QS, we need to look deeper into the $\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=0$ condition. As discussed in Appendix A, if QS were exact, we would have the same characteristics as axisymmetry. However, unlike the axisymmetric problem, the QS problem is intrinsically overdetermined and three-dimensional. With this in mind, we now motivate the PP as a criterion that allows one to look for robust quasisymmetric systems.

In axisymmetry, all field lines are equivalent, and the TW frame, where $H=0$ , is the same for all $\alpha$ . Regarding the effect on the singularities, this implies that the dependence of $B$ on the field line label is precisely the same for each singularity, which amounts to a trivial rigid shift of the frame. However, in a generic approximate 3D QS, the geometry and $B$ are strongly coupled. Due to the overdetermined nature, the $\bm{u}\cdot\bm{\nabla}B=0$ condition can only be approximately satisfied. As a consequence, the TW frame $H=0$ is, in general, different for different field lines. Thus, the $\alpha$ dependence of the singularities of $\partial_{\ell}B$ varies from field line to field line. Since these movable singularities can be critical, single-valuedness of $B$ is harder to achieve. However, when we demand the PP, the moving singularities are not critical, which respects the single-valuedness of $B$ . As shown in Sections V and VI, every numerically optimized quasisymmetric stellarator has the PP. Furthermore, as the optimization progresses, the PP emerges quickly and is maintained. Therefore, we argue that the PP is necessary and sufficient for obtaining robust QS in a 3D stellarator using numerical optimization methods, where single-valuedness and periodicity of $B$ are enforced directly using a Fourier representation.

Finally, we note that none of the above arguments required knowledge of the exact force balance condition. The roots of the polynomial in (21) that determine the zeros of $(\partial_{\ell}B)$ can vary with the flux surface label, and force balance determines their profiles. We explore the behavior of the roots of $(\partial_{\ell}B)^{2}$ in the next section, in the context of numerically optimized quasisymmetric stellarator equilibria.

## IV Reduced dimensionality of quasisymmetric $B$
