In the following, we will employ (5) specifically for a fixed-boundary vacuum field to formulate quasisymmetry on the boundary.

## 4 Application of adjoint formalism to vacuum fields

Consider a vacuum magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ in a toroidal domain $\mathcal{V}$ bounded by the surface $\mathcal{S}=\partial\mathcal{V}$ . As the vacuum magnetic field is curl-free, it can be expressed as $\mathbf{B}=\nabla\Phi$ , with the scalar potential $\Phi$ . Because we consider a simple torus $\mathcal{V}$ , the most general form for the scalar potential is $\Phi=G(\omega+\phi)$ , where $G$ is a constant, $\omega$ is a single-valued function on $\mathcal{S}$ , and $\phi$ is an arbitrary toroidal angle. By integrating the magnetic field along a toroidal loop around the torus, the constant $G$ is found to be proportional to the net external current through the ‘hole’ of the torus.

As the magnetic field is divergence-less, the magnetic scalar potential satisfies the Laplace equation. The field’s normal component is constrained to vanish on $\mathcal{S}$ by imposing a Neumann boundary condition on the magnetic scalar potential. Further prescribing e.g. $G$ , or the toroidal flux, guarantees a unique solution to Laplace’s equation. We herein opt to hold the toroidal flux fixed, although the shape derivative $\delta G[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ will not appear in this study due to our normalisation of the figure of merit for quasisymmetry (23). A different choice of normalisation would lead to an additional contribution proportional to $\delta G[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ in the shape derivative of the Lagrangian.

For convenience, we define the normalised magnetic field $\mathbf{\breve{B}}$ as

$$ \mathbf{\breve{B}}\equiv\mathbf{B}/G=\nabla\big(\omega+\phi\big). $$

Let us further assume the toroidal angle $\phi$ to be the azimuthal angle in cylindrical coordinates, satisfying $\Updelta\phi=0$ in the domain of interest. We can thus write

$$ \displaystyle\nabla\cdot\mathbf{\breve{B}}=\Updelta\omega=0\qquad\qquad\qquad\mathrm{in}\; \displaystyle\mathcal{V}, \displaystyle\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=\nabla(\omega+\phi)\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=0\qquad\mathrm{on}\; \displaystyle\mathcal{S}, $$

with $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}$ the normal unit vector on $\mathcal{S}$ . Furthermore, the shape derivative $\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\Updelta(\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}])=0\qquad\qquad\mathrm{in}\; \displaystyle\mathcal{V}, \displaystyle\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\delta\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}[\delta\mathbf{x}]+\nabla(\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}])\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}+(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=0\quad\mathrm{on}\; \displaystyle\mathcal{S}, $$

where the Laplace equation is obtained from noting the commutative property of shape and spatial derivatives, and the normal boundary condition on $\delta\omega$ was derived in e.g. Sokołowski & Zolésio (1992, §3.2). The shape derivative of the normal vector $\delta\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=-\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})$ is derived in App. A.3.

Evaluating the rotational transform and quasisymmetry figures of merit further requires the solution to the straight field line equation

$$ 0=\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\qquad\mathrm{on}\;\mathcal{S}, $$

with the field line label

$$ \alpha\equiv\theta-\iota\phi+\lambda(\theta,\phi), $$

where $\theta$ is a general poloidal angle, $\lambda$ is a single-valued function of $\theta$ and $\phi$ , and $\iota$ is a scalar. Note that both $\lambda$ and $\iota$ are defined on the boundary $\mathcal{S}$ only, through (10).

Let us define the Lagrangian corresponding to an arbitrary objective function $f(\mathcal{S},\omega,\iota,\lambda)$ ,

$$ \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{S},\omega,q_{\omega},\iota,\lambda,q_{\alpha})=f(\mathcal{S},\omega,\iota,\lambda)+\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{S},\omega,q_{\omega})+\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S},\omega,\iota,\lambda,q_{\alpha}), $$

with the weak form of the Laplace equation (7a)

$$ \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{S},\omega,q_{\omega})=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;q_{\omega}\Updelta\omega, $$

and the weak form of the straight field line equation (9) normalised by $G$

$$ \mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S},\omega,\iota,\lambda,q_{\alpha})=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha. $$

As explained in §2, $q_{\omega}$ and $q_{\alpha}$ act as Lagrange multipliers: making the Lagrangian (11) stationary with respect to $\delta q_{\omega}[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ and $\delta q_{\alpha}[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ ensures that the Laplace (7a) and straight field line (9) equations are satisfied, respectively. These trivial variations are omitted in the following under the assumption that (7a) and (9) are satisfied, thus considering only the implicit dependencies of $\delta\mathcal{L}[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ on $\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ , $\delta\iota[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ , and $\delta\lambda[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ to obtain the adjoint equations for $q_{\omega}$ and $q_{\alpha}$ .

First, the shape derivative of $\mathcal{M}$ (12), derived in App. B.1, is

$$ \delta\mathcal{M}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}]\Updelta q_{\omega}-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\bigg[\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}]\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}-(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla q_{\omega}\bigg]. $$

Second, the shape derivative of $\mathcal{N}$ (13), derived in App. B.2, is

$$ \displaystyle\delta\mathcal{N}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\int_{\mathcal{S}} \displaystyle\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\bigg[-\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}]\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(q_{\alpha}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right)-\delta\iota[\delta\mathbf{x}]\;q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\phi \displaystyle-\delta\lambda[\delta\mathbf{x}]\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right)+(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})q_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right)\bigg]. $$

The tangential gradient $\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\cdot)$ and tangential divergence $\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot(\cdot)$ operators are defined in App. A.1.

We now proceed by computing the shape derivatives of two objective functions, first targeting a given rotational transform value on $\mathcal{S}$ (§4.1), and second targeting quasi-symmetry on $\mathcal{S}$ with a given helicity value (§4.2). We will then be able to evaluate the shape derivative of the Lagrangian (11), yielding the adjoint equations and shape gradient formulas. Numerical verification and example shape gradients are shown for each figure of merit.

### 4.1 Rotational transform objective function

Before evaluating the more complicated shape gradient for the quasisymmetry figure of merit in §4.2, we consider a simple figure of merit targeting a given target rotational transform $\iota_{T}$ on the surface $\mathcal{S}$ . We thus define

$$ f_{\iota}(\iota)=\frac{1}{2}(\iota-\iota_{T})^{2}, $$

where $\iota$ is the rotational transform on $\mathcal{S}$ , obtained by solving the straight field line equation (9). The shape derivative of $f_{\iota}$ is simply

$$ \delta f_{\iota}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\delta\iota[\delta\mathbf{x}]\;(\iota-\iota_{T}). $$

By combining (14), (15), and (17), we obtain the shape derivative of the Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{\iota}$ [(11) with $f=f_{\iota}$ ],

$$ \displaystyle\delta\mathcal{L} {}_{\iota}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}]\;\Updelta q_{\omega}-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}]\bigg[\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}+\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Big(q_{\alpha}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\Big)\bigg] \displaystyle-\delta\iota[\delta\mathbf{x}]\;\bigg[\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\phi+(\iota-\iota_{T})\bigg]-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\delta\lambda[\delta\mathbf{x}]\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Big(q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\Big) \displaystyle+\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\bigg[\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\mathbf{\breve{B}}+q_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right)\bigg]\Bigg]. $$

First, we obtain the adjoint equation for $q_{\alpha}$ by requiring the second line of (18) to vanish,

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Big(q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\Big)=0, \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\phi+(\iota-\iota_{T})=0, $$

with both equations defined on $\mathcal{S}$ . Using (30), the surface integral of (19a) yields $0=\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}$ , which is consistent with the boundary condition on the magnetic field (7b). The first equation (19a) can be recast in the form of a magnetic differential equation $\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla q_{\alpha}=-q_{\alpha}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ , while the second equation (19b) is an integral condition on $q_{\alpha}$ that ensures uniqueness of the solution.

Second, the adjoint equation for $q_{\omega}$ is obtained by requiring the first line of (18) to vanish,

$$ \displaystyle\Updelta q_{\omega}=0\qquad\qquad\qquad\mathrm{in}\; \displaystyle\mathcal{V}, \displaystyle\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=-\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Big(q_{\alpha}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\Big)\qquad\mathrm{on}\; \displaystyle\mathcal{S}. $$

Like the magnetic potential $\omega$ , the adjoint variable $q_{\omega}$ satisfies the Laplace equation in $\mathcal{V}$ (20a). However, contrary to $\omega$ , $q_{\omega}$ has a non-zero normal boundary condition on $\mathcal{S}$ (20b), which notably depends on the straight field line adjoint variable $q_{\alpha}$ . Equations (20b) and (20a) are consistent, as $\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\Updelta q_{\omega}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=0$ , by (30).

Finally, the remaining contribution from the last line of (18) yields the shape gradient

$$ \mathcal{G_{\iota}}=\frac{1}{G}\Big[\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla q_{\omega}+q_{\alpha}\big(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\big)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\Big], $$

with $\delta\mathcal{L}_{\iota}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;\mathcal{G_{\iota}}$ .

We now calculate the shape gradient numerically and verify it against a finite-difference evaluation. The solutions to Laplace’s equation for the vacuum magnetic field (7a) and adjoint equation for $q_{\omega}$ (20a) are calculated with the SPEC code (Hudson et al., 2012), employing the new Zernike polynomial implementation (Qu et al., 2020). In all results shown, the radial resolution $L_{\mathrm{rad}}$ in SPEC is tied to the poloidal Fourier resolution $M_{\mathrm{pol}}$ through $L_{\mathrm{rad}}=M_{\mathrm{pol}}+4$ . The solutions to the straight field line and $q_{\alpha}$ adjoint equations are obtained with a Fourier-Galerkin spectral solver.

As mentioned in §2, errors in the adjoint shape gradient are introduced by the assumption that the constraint and adjoint PDEs are exactly satisfied. In practice, these PDEs are solved only approximately, limited by the finite Fourier and radial resolution, such that a reduction of the error with increasing resolution is to be expected.

### 4.2 Quasisymmetry objective function

For a general (non-vacuum) magnetic field with nested flux surfaces, quasisymmetry can be expressed as

$$ \frac{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\psi\times\nabla B}{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla B}=-\frac{MG+NI}{N-\iota M}, $$

where $I$ is the net toroidal plasma current and $N/M$ is the helicity of the field strength in Boozer coordinates, see e.g. Helander (2014). For the vacuum field considered here, $I=0$ . In the following, we will not consider quasi-poloidal symmetry, i.e. we will assume $M\neq 0$ . If desired, it would be straight-forward to extend the derived results to include the case $M=0$ .

For magnetic fields with globally nested flux surfaces labelled by $\psi$ , (22) is defined globally. However, we are considering a generally non-integrable field, assuming only that the boundary $\mathcal{S}$ is a flux surface. Using the generalised toroidal flux gradient defined in (5), we are able to define quasisymmetry on the isolated flux surface $\mathcal{S}$ , leading to the quasisymmetry (QS) objective function

$$ f_{\mathrm{QS}}(\mathcal{S},\omega,\iota,\lambda)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}^{2}(\omega,\iota,\lambda), $$

with

$$ v_{\mathrm{QS}}=\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}\left(\iota-N/M\right). $$

If $f_{\mathrm{QS}}=0$ and the field is integrable in the neighbourhood of $\mathcal{S}$ , (22) will be satisfied on $\mathcal{S}$ , i.e. the field is quasisymmetric on the boundary.

The shape derivative of $f_{\mathrm{QS}}$ is derived in App. B.3, with the final expression given in (62). Combined with the shape derivatives of $\mathcal{M}$ (14) and $\mathcal{N}$ (15), the shape derivative of the Lagrangian (11) with the quasisymmetric figure of merit follows (64).

Requiring the Lagrangian to be stationary with respect to variations in $\iota$ and $\lambda$ , the first two lines of (64) yield the adjoint equations for $q_{\alpha}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Big(q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\Big)=-\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left[\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\left(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}\;\frac{\iota-N/M}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}\right)\right], \displaystyle 0=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\left\{q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\phi+v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}\left[\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\phi}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}(\iota-N/M)+1\right]\right\}. $$

Similarly to the rotational transform objective function case, $q_{\alpha}$ satisfies a magnetic differential equation (25a) on $\mathcal{S}$ , with integral condition (25b). By (30), the surface integral of (25a) is consistent with the magnetic field’s normal component vanishing on the boundary (7b).

Furthermore, requiring the Lagrangian to be stationary with respect to variations in $\omega$ , we obtain the adjoint equations for $q_{\omega}$ from the third and fourth lines of (64)

$$ \displaystyle\Updelta q_{\omega} \displaystyle=0\qquad\qquad\qquad\mathrm{in}\;\mathcal{V}, \displaystyle\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}} \displaystyle=-\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Bigg\{q_{\alpha}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha+v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}-\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}}{\breve{B}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}) \displaystyle+\left(\iota-N/M\right)\left[v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\times\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{\breve{B}}v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\right)\right]\Bigg\}\quad\text{ on }\mathcal{S}. $$

Again, $q_{\omega}$ satisfies the Laplace equation in $\mathcal{V}$ (26a), with a normal boundary condition on $\mathcal{S}$ that is the tangential divergence of a vector tangential to the surface (26b). The boundary condition (26b) is consistent with the Laplace equation, as $\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\Updelta q_{\omega}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=0$ , by (30).

Finally, we obtain the shape gradient from the last three lines of (64),

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{G} {}_{\mathrm{QS}}=-(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B})\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right)-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\left(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B} \displaystyle+\left(\iota-N/M\right)\;\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B}\cdot\left[\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\left(\frac{v_{\mathrm{QS}}}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}\right)+\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\left(\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}-h\right)\right] \displaystyle+\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla q_{\omega}+q_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\right)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha+\frac{h}{2}v_{\mathrm{QS}}^{2}, $$

with $\delta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QS}}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;\mathcal{G_{\mathrm{QS}}}$ , and $h$ the summed curvature.

## 5 Conclusions

In this work, we derived the adjoint equations and shape gradient for the rotational transform and quasisymmetry of a vacuum field on a surface. The shape gradients allow fast computation of derivatives with respect to the parameters that describe the geometry of the surface, which are used in optimisation and sensitivity analyses. For a boundary represented by $N$ parameters, the speed-up from the adjoint method is $O(N)$ compared to a finite-difference evaluation.

This should enable future use of codes such as SPEC (Hudson et al., 2012) in optimisation calculations, which was hitherto neglected in favour of the more widely-used VMEC code (Hirshman et al., 1986). Contrary to VMEC, SPEC does not rely on the assumption of nested flux surfaces and can therefore model stochastic and island regions. In practice, employing adjoint methods and computing derivatives of quantities arising from ideal MHS equilibria is challenging, as the linearised MHS equilibrium equations possess regular singular points at every rational surface that resonates with the perturbation. These challenges can be avoided by the use of alternative equilibrium models, such as force-free magnetic fields, or the vacuum fields considered in this work. The generality of the results presented herein would also allow for their implementation in other solvers such as BIEST (Malhotra et al., 2019). It is left for future work to extend the vacuum field results presented herein to the more general force-free fields modeled by SPEC. Furthermore, the adjoint methods for vacuum fields introduced in this work could be fruitfully applied to other optimisation problems, e.g. in neoclassical transport calculations.

It is generally believed that exact quasisymmetry cannot be obtained exactly in a finite volume as near-axis expansions lead to an an overdetermined system of equations (Garren & Boozer, 1991), although that can be resolved by allowing for an anisotropic plasma pressure (Rodríguez & Bhattacharjee, 2021a; Rodríguez & Bhattacharjee, 2021b). Exact quasisymmetry on a surface is thought generally possible (Garren & Boozer, 1991; Plunk & Helander, 2018); and indeed, a vacuum solution near axisymmetry was recently found (Sengupta et al., 2021). The shape gradient for quasisymmetry derived in this work could be used to numerically probe the existence of quasisymmetric solutions on a surface that are not close to axisymmetry. For this purpose, the shape gradient for the rotational transform objective function (21) could be used to avoid the axisymmetric solution at $\iota=0$ , or also to avoid low order rationals. Furthermore, the shape gradients derived herein could be used to investigate if and how optimisation for quasisymmetry and for the rotational transform compete with each other. Finally, combining the derivatives of quasisymmetry and rotational transform with previously obtained derivatives of coil shapes (Hudson et al., 2018) and island size (Geraldini et al., 2021) should, in principle, allow for the efficient search of a stellarator configuration with significant rotational transform, good integrability and neoclassical confinement at the boundary, realised by simple coils.

## Appendix A Basics of shape differential calculus

This appendix aims to provide a brief introduction to calculus on surfaces, mainly providing useful identities required in the derivation of the adjoint equations, without strict mathematical rigour. For more details on the subject, we refer the interested reader to Walker (2015).

In this section, we take $\mathcal{S}=\partial\mathcal{V}$ to be a closed two-dimensional surface bounding the volume $\mathcal{V}$ . Let $f$ and $\mathbf{v}$ be respectively scalar and vector functions defined on $\mathcal{S}$ . The extensions of these functions to a neighbourhood of $\mathcal{S}$ are denoted by $\tilde{f}$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{v}}$ . Note that $f$ and $\mathbf{v}$ can also be functions defined in $\mathcal{V}$ , in which case $\tilde{f}$ and $\mathbf{\tilde{v}}$ are chosen to be equal to $f$ and $\mathbf{v}$ , respectively; the tangential gradient $\nabla_{\Upgamma}f$ and tangential divergence $\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\mathbf{v}$ remain defined on $\mathcal{S}$ .

### A.1 Differential operators on surfaces

The tangential gradient $\nabla_{\Upgamma}$ can be defined in terms of an extension as

$$ \nabla_{\Upgamma}f\equiv\nabla\tilde{f}-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\tilde{f}\right), $$

where $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}$ is the unit normal vector on $\mathcal{S}$ . The tangential gradient can thus simply be viewed as the component of the three-dimensional gradient tangential to the surface, satisfying $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}f=0$ .

Similarly to the tangential gradient, the tangential divergence $\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot$ can be defined in terms of an extension as

$$ \nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\mathbf{v}=\nabla\cdot\mathbf{\tilde{v}}-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\tilde{v}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}. $$

The related divergence theorem is particularly useful in our derivation of the adjoint equations,

$$ \int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\mathbf{v}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;h\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\mathbf{v}\;, $$

where $h$ is the summed curvature, and $\mathbf{v}$ is assumed to be single-valued. In particular, it follows from (30) that $\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$ for a single-valued $\mathbf{v}$ with $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$ .

### A.2 Transport theorems

To evaluate the shape derivative of the Lagrangian (see § 2) and obtain the adjoint equations, we need expressions for the shape derivatives of volume and surface integrals. These are called transport theorems. First, for a volume functional

$$ J_{V}=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;f, $$

the shape derivative of $J_{V}$ is given by

$$ \delta J_{V}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\delta f[\delta\mathbf{x}]+\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;f. $$

Second, for a surface functional

$$ J_{S}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;f, $$

the shape derivative of $J_{S}$ is

$$ \delta J_{S}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\Big[\delta f[\delta\mathbf{x}]+(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\tilde{f}+hf\right)\Big]. $$

In both (32) and (34), the first term originates from the direct perturbation of the integrand while the second term accounts for the change of the boundary.

### A.3 Normal extension and the normal vector’s shape derivative

The signed distance function $b$ is defined in a sufficiently small neighbourhood of $\mathcal{S}$ as

$$ b(\mathbf{r})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\text{dist}(\mathbf{r},\mathcal{S}),\hskip 12.80365pt\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\mathcal{V}\\
0,\hskip 48.36958pt\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{S}\\
-\text{dist}(\mathbf{r},\mathcal{S}),\hskip 5.69046pt\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{V}\end{array}\right.. $$

Here, $\text{dist}(\mathbf{r},\mathcal{S})$ is the closest distance from a point $\mathbf{r}$ to the surface $\mathcal{S}$ .

For quantities defined only on the surface $\mathcal{S}$ , like the normal vector $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}$ or the field line label $\alpha$ , one is free to choose an arbitrary extension to the neighbourhood of $\mathcal{S}$ . Any final result (e.g. the shape gradient or adjoint equations) should be independent of this choice. A particularly convenient choice is the normal extension $\tilde{f}(\mathbf{x})=f(\mathbf{x}-b(\mathbf{x})\nabla b(\mathbf{x}))$ , as it implies $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\tilde{f}=0$ on $\mathcal{S}$ . Vector functions $\mathbf{v}$ can be similarly extended.

The signed distance function can also be used to express the unit normal vector on $\mathcal{S}$ as $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=\nabla b$ . Let us define

$$ J_{n}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\chi\;b=0, $$

with an arbitrary function $\chi$ . The transport theorem (34) then yields

$$ 0=\delta J_{n}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\chi\Big[\delta b[\delta\mathbf{x}]+(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\Big], $$

which must hold for any $\chi$ , such that $\delta b[\delta\mathbf{x}]=-\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}$ . Then, the shape derivative of the normal vector follows as $\delta\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}[\delta\mathbf{x}]=\nabla(\delta b[\delta\mathbf{x}])=-\nabla(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})$ . If the unit normal vector is normally extended off $\mathcal{S}$ , as is assumed in the remainder of this paper, it follows from (28) that

$$ \delta\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=-\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}). $$

Note also that the summed curvature $h$ and normal vector are related through $\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=h$ .

## Appendix B Derivations of shape derivatives

For ease of notation, we will in the following derivations write shape derivatives without the $[\delta\mathbf{x}]$ bracket, e.g. $\delta\omega[\delta\mathbf{x}]\rightarrow\delta\omega$ , and drop tildes for extensions off the surface $\mathcal{S}$ . Furthermore, we will take the field line label $\alpha$ (10) and the normal vector $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}$ to be normally extended off $\mathcal{S}$ , such that $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\tilde{\alpha}=0$ and $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\tilde{\hat{n}}}=0$ , see App. A.3 for more details on normal extensions.

### B.1 Weak form of Laplace equation

The weak form of the Laplace equation, previously given in (12), can be partially integrated to facilitate the calculation of the shape derivative,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;q_{\omega}\Updelta\omega=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\omega\Updelta q_{\omega}+\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\left(q_{\omega}\nabla\omega-\omega\nabla q_{\omega}\right)\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\omega\Updelta q_{\omega}-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\left(q_{\omega}\nabla\phi+\omega\nabla q_{\omega}\right)\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}, $$

where the boundary condition on the magnetic field (7b) was used in the last equality. Using the transport theorems (32) and (34), the shape derivative of (39) is computed to be

$$ \displaystyle\delta\mathcal{M} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\delta\omega\Updelta q_{\omega}+\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\bigg\{-\delta\omega\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}-(q_{\omega}\nabla\phi+\omega\nabla q_{\omega})\cdot\delta\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}} \displaystyle+(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\Big[\omega\Updelta q_{\omega}-(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla+h)\left(q_{\omega}\nabla\phi\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}+\omega\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\right)\Big]\bigg\}. $$

The term involving the normal vector’s shape derivative $\delta\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}$ can be further simplified using (38),

$$ \displaystyle-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;(q_{\omega}\nabla\phi+\omega\nabla q_{\omega})\cdot\delta\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\left[-(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot(q_{\omega}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\phi+\omega\nabla_{\Upgamma}q_{\omega})\right] \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\bigg[h\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot(q_{\omega}\nabla\phi+\omega\nabla q_{\omega})+\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot(q_{\omega}\nabla\nabla\phi+\omega\nabla\nabla q_{\omega})\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}-\omega\Updelta q_{\omega}-\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\mathbf{\breve{B}}\bigg], $$

where the surface divergence theorem (30) was used in the second equality. Inserting this expression back into (40), the shape derivative of $\mathcal{M}$ simplifies to

$$ \delta\mathcal{M}=\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\delta\omega\Updelta q_{\omega}-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\bigg[\delta\omega\nabla q_{\omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}-(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla q_{\omega}\bigg], $$

where we used (6).

### B.2 Weak form of straight field line equation

The shape derivative of the straight field line equation’s weak form (13) follows from the transport theorem (34), as well as the shape derivatives of the field line label $\delta\alpha=-\phi\;\delta\iota+\delta\lambda$ and the normalised magnetic field $\delta\mathbf{\breve{B}}=\nabla(\delta\omega)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\delta\mathcal{N}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\; \displaystyle\left[q_{\alpha}\nabla(\delta\omega)\cdot\nabla\alpha+q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\left(\nabla(\delta\lambda)-\delta\iota\nabla\phi\right)+(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\left(q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\alpha\right)\right], $$

where the summed curvature term in (34) vanishes here due to the straight field line equation (9). The first term is partially integrated using (30),

$$ \int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;q_{\alpha}\nabla(\delta\omega)\cdot\nabla\alpha=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;q_{\alpha}\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\omega)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\left[-\delta\omega\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(q_{\alpha}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right)\right], $$

as well as the $\delta\lambda$ term,

$$ \int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla(\delta\lambda)=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\lambda)=-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\delta\lambda\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right). $$

The last term in (43) can also be simplified using (9),

$$ \displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\left(q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\alpha\right) \displaystyle=q_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\alpha+\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\nabla\alpha\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\right)=q_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\right)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha. $$

The shape derivative of $\mathcal{N}$ (43) finally reduces to

$$ \displaystyle\delta\mathcal{N}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\bigg[ \displaystyle-\delta\omega\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(q_{\alpha}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right)-\delta\iota\;q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\phi-\delta\lambda\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right) \displaystyle+(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;q_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\right)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\bigg]. $$

### B.3 Quasisymmetry figure of merit

Using the transport theorem (34), we can express the shape derivative of the quasisymmetry figure of merit (23) as

$$ \delta f_{\mathrm{QS}}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\Big\{v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\delta v_{\mathrm{QS}}+\frac{1}{2}(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla+h)v_{\mathrm{QS}}^{2}\Big\}. $$

First, note $\delta\mathbf{\breve{B}}=\nabla(\delta\omega)$ , which also gives the shape derivative of the normalised magnetic field strength as

$$ \delta\breve{B}=\delta\left(\sqrt{\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\mathbf{\breve{B}}}\right)=\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla(\delta\omega)}{\breve{B}}. $$

Furthermore, recalling $|\overline{\nabla\psi}|/G=\breve{B}/\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}$ from (5), we obtain

$$ \delta\left(\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\right)=\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\;\left[\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla(\delta\omega)}{\breve{B}^{2}}-\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\left(-\delta\iota\nabla_{\Upgamma}\phi+\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\lambda)\right)}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}\right]. $$

Using (49), (50), (8b) and (38), the shape derivative of $v_{\mathrm{QS}}$ (24) can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\delta v_{\mathrm{QS}} \displaystyle=\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\omega)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}+(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B})\left[-(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}+\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\right] \displaystyle+\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\left(\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\omega)}{\breve{B}}\right)-\delta\iota\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\;\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}-\left(\iota-N/M\right)\;\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G} \displaystyle\times\Bigg[\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\omega)\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B})+\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\left(\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\omega)}{\breve{B}}\right) \displaystyle+\left(\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\omega)}{\breve{B}^{2}}-\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\left(-\delta\iota\nabla_{\Upgamma}\phi+\nabla_{\Upgamma}(\delta\lambda)\right)}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}\right)\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\Bigg]. $$

The first term in (48) can then be partially integrated to

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\delta v_{\mathrm{QS}}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\Bigg\{\delta\omega\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Bigg[-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}+\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}}{\breve{B}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}) \displaystyle+\left(\iota-N/M\right)\Bigg(\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\times\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}-\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}}{\breve{B}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\bigg(\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\bigg) \displaystyle+v_{\mathrm{QS}}\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}}{\tilde{B^{2}}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\Bigg)\Bigg]-\delta\iota\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\left[\left(\iota-N/M\right)\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\phi}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}+1\right] \displaystyle-\delta\lambda\;\left(\iota-N/M\right)\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Bigg[v_{\mathrm{QS}}\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\Bigg] \displaystyle-(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\Bigg[\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\left(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}\right)-\left(\iota-N/M\right)\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Bigg(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times(\nabla\breve{B}-\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B})\Bigg)\Bigg]\Bigg\}, $$

The terms in the last line can be simplified, first using

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\left(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}\right)=(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B})\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla v_{\mathrm{QS}}+v_{\mathrm{QS}}\left(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}+\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\nabla\breve{B}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\right). $$

Furthermore, note that

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B})=-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B})\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}, $$

where we used (29), $\nabla\times\mathbf{\breve{B}}=0$ and $\nabla\times\nabla\breve{B}=0$ ; and

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\Bigg(\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\Bigg) \displaystyle=-\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{\breve{B}}\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B})+\frac{1}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}\right), $$

using (28). The terms of the last parenthesis in (52) now simplify to

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Bigg(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B}\Bigg) \displaystyle=\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\bigg[\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B}\cdot\left(\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\left(\frac{v_{\mathrm{QS}}}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}\right)-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\frac{\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}}{\breve{B}}\right)-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B})\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\bigg], $$

and

$$ \nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Bigg(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\Bigg)=h\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}, $$

where we used the fact that $\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}$ is normal to the surface, and $\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}=h$ .

We now turn to the normal derivative of $v_{\mathrm{QS}}$ , the second term in (48). Using the fact that $\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}$ and $\alpha$ are normally extended, we can write

$$ \boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B})=-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B})\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}} $$

and

$$ \boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}=\frac{\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}=\frac{\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\nabla\alpha\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}=-\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}, $$

such that

$$ \boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\left(\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\right)=\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\left[\frac{\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}}{\breve{B}}+\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}\right]. $$

This allows us to express the normal derivative of $v_{\mathrm{QS}}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla v_{\mathrm{QS}}=\;\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}+\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\nabla\breve{B}\cdot\mathbf{\breve{B}} \displaystyle-(\iota-N/M)\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\left[-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B})\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}+\left(\frac{\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}}{\breve{B}}+\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}\right)\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}\right]. $$

Combining (48), (52) (and simplifications thereafter) and (61), the shape derivative of $f_{\mathrm{QS}}$ can finally be expressed as

$$ \displaystyle\delta \displaystyle f_{\mathrm{QS}}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\Bigg\{\delta\omega\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Bigg[-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}+\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}}{\breve{B}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}) \displaystyle+\left(\iota-N/M\right)\Bigg(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\times\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{\breve{B}}v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\right)\Bigg)\Bigg] \displaystyle-\delta\iota\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\left[\left(\iota-N/M\right)\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\phi}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}+1\right] \displaystyle-\delta\lambda\;\left(\iota-N/M\right)\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left[v_{\mathrm{QS}}\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\right] \displaystyle+(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;\Bigg[\left(\iota-N/M\right)\;\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B}\cdot\left(\nabla_{\Upgamma}v_{\mathrm{QS}}-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}\right) \displaystyle+\frac{h}{2}v_{\mathrm{QS}}^{2}-(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B})\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right)-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\left(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B} \displaystyle-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}\;\left(\iota-N/M\right)\left(\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}-h\right)\Bigg]\Bigg\}, $$

where we used

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}=\left(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}+\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\mathbf{\breve{B}}\;(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B}). $$

$$ \displaystyle\delta \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QS}}=-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\delta\lambda\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left[q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}+\left(\iota-N/M\right)v_{\mathrm{QS}}\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}\;\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\right] \displaystyle-\delta\iota\;\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\Bigg\{q_{\alpha}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\phi+v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}\left[\left(\iota-N/M\right)\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\phi}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}+1\right]\Bigg\} \displaystyle+\int_{\mathcal{V}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V\;\delta\omega\;\Updelta q_{\omega}-\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;\delta\omega\Bigg\{\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla q_{\omega}+\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\Bigg[-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}+\frac{\mathbf{\breve{B}}}{\breve{B}}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}) \displaystyle+\left(\iota-N/M\right)\Bigg(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\times\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\;\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{\breve{B}}v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\frac{\overline{\nabla\psi}}{G}\right)\Bigg)\Bigg]\Bigg\} \displaystyle+\int_{\mathcal{S}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\;(\delta\boldsymbol{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}})\;\Bigg\{-(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\breve{B})\nabla_{\Upgamma}\cdot\left(v_{\mathrm{QS}}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right)-v_{\mathrm{QS}}\;\left(\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}-\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}\right)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\breve{B} \displaystyle+\left(\iota-N/M\right)\frac{|\overline{\nabla\psi}|}{G}\mathbf{\breve{B}}\times\nabla\breve{B}\cdot\left[\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}\nabla_{\Upgamma}\left(\frac{v_{\mathrm{QS}}}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}}\right)+\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\;v_{\mathrm{QS}}\left(\frac{\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha}{\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha\right\rvert}^{2}}-h\right)\right] \displaystyle+\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla q_{\omega}+q_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{\breve{B}}-\mathbf{\breve{B}}\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol{\hat{\mathrm{n}}}\right)\cdot\nabla_{\Upgamma}\alpha+\frac{h}{2}v_{\mathrm{QS}}^{2},\Bigg\}.
